The House resumed from Monday, March 2, consideration of the motion of Mr. Wilson (Etobicoke Centre) that this House approve in general the budgetary policy of the Government, and the amendment of Mr. Garneau (p. 3594).

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak to the amendment moved by the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau).

During the parliamentary break last week I and several of my colleagues from the Upper House had the occasion to tour the four provinces of western Canada as part of a caucus investigation into the economic problems and opportunities for development there. That opportunity to visit, immediately upon the heels of the Budget, revealed clearly to us the very serious gap between the hard economic reality of western Canada and the total lack of commitment or response by the Government of Canada to those new realities.
We began by meeting with groups of farmers in the Province of Manitoba. These people, who had been in the farm business for 30 or 40 years, had one basic message, that they had to leave their farms. They can no longer make money. Their sons and daughters do not want to take over the land. A farmer who has 900 to 1,000 acres of good production land was talking about walking away from it this fall because each year he experiences a shortfall of $12,000, $15,000 or $20,000. Although the grain payment has been loudly trumpeted in this House as the solution to the problem, the farm community of western Canada sees no solution in sight. Farmers are terrified
March 3, 1987
by the changes in the international market, the lack of security for the future, and the escalation in costs.
We also spoke to a number of university students. They are facing quotas, for the first time in the history of public universities in western Canada; controls on the number of students able to attend. As the restrictions grow, due to budget restraints, universities will no longer be a channel for mobility for working class young men and women. They will in fact become elitist organizations because of the restrictions. That is to say nothing of the cut-backs in research. The faculty of engineering at the University of Manitoba, a well respected major faculty which is trying to be at the forefront of research and development, has an operating budget of $1 million a year.
We met with people from the oil industry in Alberta who perhaps presented the most glum and most desperate set of circumstances that one could possibly imagine. In 1985 there were 12,564 wells drilled. In 1987 they expect just a few more than 3,000 to be drilled. Their message was that Canada, under the present low level of investment in the oil and gas sector, will no longer be able to maintain its reserves. It will increasingly be forced into a position of dependency on imported oil and gas because no capital investment is going into the oil and gas sector, even to maintain our level of reserves.
We talked to the business community of British Columbia. Mr. Makin came before us. He said that in 1981 capital investment in British Columbia was at $12 billion. By 1986 it had fallen to $8 billion and was decreasing even more.
These people basically suggested that the economy of western Canada is not in a healthy state. Commodity resources are suffering from the depression of world-wide prices. The business community is not getting the investment it needs to generate new production. The universities and research centres are being cut back from opportunities to develop new products and innovation. We kept being asked where the leadership of the federal Government is to provide answers to these problems. When they read the Budget papers they found no answer. The Budget was not a document, economic blueprint or agenda for change. At best, it was a chartered accountant's tote sheet and, at worst, simply a public relations exercise. There was nothing in there which would provide basic political decisions upon which economic decisions could be made.
I believe this demonstrates that the Government has lost the fundamental Canadian requirement to have a political economy recognizing the interchange between political decision-making and economic decision-making. This country was not built by the free flow of market forces, but by a series of political decisions setting out investments, guidelines and directions in which the market-place could operate.
We no longer have a Government which believes in a political economy. We no longer have a Government which recognizes that it shares the responsibility to provide signals to the market-place, to compensate where the market-place is not operational, and to provide a direction and thrust to the
March 3, 1987

economy, whether by building a railroad, providing signals in the energy area, or attempting to deal with incredible changes on the international market-place. There is nothing in the document, absolutely no reflection that there is a hard, tough economic reality facing Canadians and that the federal Government must accept some responsibility for providing leadership in that area.
We received close to 100 representations from a wide variety of interest groups. Through those, certain messages began to come through about the structural changes taking place in the Canadian economy. Perhaps the most frightening for western Canadians, as it would be in other parts of Canada, is the decoupling between the resource economy, the commodity markets of Canada, and industrial production.
According to all the economic textbooks, there used to be an interrelationship between prices, growth, employment and between commodity markets and industrial markets. That is no longer the case because it has been severed. The depression in commodity prices, the slow-down in production and the retardation in employment in those areas that are based on the resource economy has not affected the industrial economy. We know that at least one part of the economy, southern Ontario, is experiencing some growth, but it is somewhat of a condemnation of the theory that a coupling of the national economy is taking place. There is no effort to stitch that national economy back together and provide for the stability or the investment in the resource economy to respond to that growth.
It is also clear from the representations we have received that there is a greater gap between new production and investment, and employment. Perhaps the harshest judgment that must be levelled against the Budget is that after four years of a growing economy the unemployment rate in this country is still near 10 per cent. In spite of the ability to recover from the world-wide recession that affected this country in the early 1980s, Canada has been one of the slowest countries to recover its employment base. There are still many people unemployed even though there have been four years of economic growth above 3 per cent or 4 per cent.
I suggest something is fundamentally wrong when the Government has only increased employment by 1 per cent or 2 per cent after four years of recovery. This problem is most directly impacting the regions of Canada rather than the central heartland, as shown by the pathos we see in places which had a booming economy but are now facing 15 per cent unemployment. Again, the Budget provides no answer to this situation.
In fact, the Estimates that were tabled yesterday reveal that there is close to $200 million in cut-backs in the job-creation programs of the Government, including cut-backs on programs for student hiring, DRIE grants of investment in those regions and even cut-backs in the commitments of the previous Government for development in those areas. This is at a time
The Budget-Mr. Axworthy
when the economies of the regions are experiencing a serious downfall.
That fact alone should warn the Government that the unemployment rate is not responding to the growth rate, but is responding unevenly by decreasing in one region, at best, while increasing in other regions during a time of so-called recovery and economic growth. Surely the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and his colleagues should have given Canadians answers to those questions, but the Budget was silent on that matter.
Another example we learned from the weeks of hearings we held is that the international economy is directly affecting the Canadian economic reality, with debt crises in third world countries, increasing prices of commodities, loss of capital flows, and other serious influences. Yet, there is no ability to respond to those influences because the Government is too obsessed with the Canada-U.S. free trade talks. One would be led to believe from reading the document carefully that we are not part of an international economy, because it did not take into account the incredible fluctuations taking place in capital markets, the fact that our trade balances in all other parts of the world are declining, and that we are losing markets in Asia, Latin America and Europe.
There has been no effort to develop new markets and new products for those areas. Western Canadians who are involved in agriculture and industry believe they can do so, but being small business people, they do not have the huge corporate budgets for those new markets and product development. They tell us that they need assistance to transfer technology, that they need science centres to test new products and develop and open new markets, and need to increase value added products in order to respond to that demand. Yet again, the Budget provides no response to that. It is no wonder that western Canadians are deeply frustrated and disappointed with this Budget.
I am sure Conservative Members have had an opportunity to read recent public opinion polls. They know that one of the important political stories in Canada today is the incredible crumbling of the Tories in western Canada. In my Province of Manitoba, for example, the Conservatives have fallen from 50 per cent support of voters to 20 per cent in a matter of a year. While I should be happy that we are leading with 44 per cent of support, the fact is that it does not reflect the fumbling performance of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) or the scandals involving the Government. The Conservatives are losing support because western Canadians are seriously disappointed that the Government is not responding to the economic crisis in western Canada. It has been unable to provide economic leadership to the problems facing Canadians.
Westerners want some assistance to meet the affects of the U.S. Farm Bill that has driven agricultural prices down 25 per cent in the last year. The Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) and the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) only say that the problem will be solved seven or eight years

March 3, 1987
The Budget-Mr. Axworthy
from now. Those producers want a clear signal that there will be a program of deficiency payments to keep our farmers in business and, at the same time, tell the Americans and Europeans that they cannot force us out of markets.
Western Canadians want a clear commitment to research and development in western Canada, rather than its withdrawal. Let me give an example from yesterday's Estimates. An ERDA agreement in the Province of Manitoba was signed in 1983, designating that province as the centre of development for urban bus research and development and manufacturing. This was identified by the province and the federal Government as an area of potential export markets. The agreement was signed for $21 million over a five-year period, but, according to the Estimates, the Government spent $17,000 in the first three years of that agreement. In other words, the Government had an opportunity to give a western province the potential to develop a new technology in an export market that is growing around the world by assisting manufacturers in that area to develop new products. Instead of using that agreement, the Government snuffed it out.
Similarly, another agreement on communications and culture was signed with Manitoba. It was designed to develop that area as a potential export market for that province. The agreement represented a $22-million commitment, but only $6 million has been spent with one year left in the agreement.
It is clear that the Minister of Finance and his colleagues are cutting back on cash flow in order to meet their deficit targets. They are cutting back on investment, jobs and potential economic development that would create new tax dollars and new revenues which would be far more productive in reducing the deficit than these mealy-mouthed, niggardly and cheap reductions we see now.
The fundamental problem facing the Government is that there is no sense of political economy which reflects the philosophy that the driving force in the economy should be full employment. We hear these great panegyric and rhetorical displays about lowering the deficit. Rather, the Government should be aiming at full employment which is the best answer to deficit reduction. The best way to deal with the fiscal framework in this country is to employ far more people. The difference between a 9.7 per cent unemployment rate and a 5 per cent unemployment rate is a 50 per cent reduction in the Government deficits and a substantial increase in opportunities for Canadians. The fact is that the Government does not have a commitment to full employment. It has not built into its decision-making process any concept that full employment must be the primary objective and goal and, therefore, the economic decisions it makes are not geared or driven by that particular purpose or judgment. That is the fundamental flaw of its whole budgetary process.
There is no concept of political economy in this case and no sense that political decisions will make a difference, just a
reliance upon this kind of laissez-faire market-place, the end result being that growth takes place only in one region and the rest of the regions suffer a serious recession to the point where they are in danger of losing their fundamental ways of making a living. That is our objection and the reason we have introduced a non-confidence motion with respect to this Budget. It is not an economic blueprint. It provides no economic leadership. It does not deal with the problems of structural change. In fact, it has no sense of goal or purpose which will give a direction to those parts of our national economy which are looking for some kind of assistance.
As long as we continue in this way, the disparity and gaps will grow wider and the sense of desperation and frustration will grow even more extreme. We can only hope that within the next 18 months to two years the Government has left to continue this absence of economic leadership, conditions will not get so bad that when we become government we will not be able to rescue it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I was rather interested in the Hon. Member's comments about agriculture in the west and deficiency payments, and so on. Not too long ago the Hon. Member sat on this side of the House. His Government had a Minister of Agriculture who refused to honour an application for assistance under the Stabilization Act for Okanagan fruit farmers for 1983-84 soft-fruit crops and the 1984 apple crop. I wonder why the Hon. Member has chosen to change his tune now that he sits on the other side of the House? The Minister of Agriculture at that time told me as a result of my questions in the House: "We are not going to pay the Okanagan farmers any stabilization payment. Let them go to the province or some other place. We are not going to help them out". The Hon. Member has now a great heart for Canadian farmers. Is it just Manitoban farmers he is interested in? How does the Hon. Member account for this sudden change in attitude? It certainly was not demonstrated when he sat on this side of the House and had the ability to do things for farmers. He slammed the door in their faces.

speechtext: Resuming debate. The Hon. Member for Lac-Saint-Jean (Mr. Cote).

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour for me to take part in the debate on this budget, because once again, our Government has shown that it knows how to keep its promises and that our desire to put the economy on a sound basis is not wishful thinking. About two weeks ago, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) brought down a budget that augured well for Canada. He has shown once again that the determination and firm attitude of this Government has helped to put the economy back on the right track. The message has been clear and consistent since September 1984. We must restore this country's fiscal responsibility and good fiscal management. The national debt must be taken in hand, the deficit brought down and Government spending brought under control.
In the third budget brought down since this Government was sworn in, these objectives have been achieved once again. For the third consecutive year, the deficit is down. We must

March 3, 1987
The Budget-Mr. Clement Cote
not forget why this politically suicidal decision to reduce the deficit was made and why we were not afraid to implement that decision. The reason was that Government involvement in the economy was about to paralyze our economic growth. Layers of regulations distorted investment decisions and business practices. Fifteen straight years of budget deficits had swollen the national debt to $200 billion. The rapid increase in the public debt made Canada's future economic prospects increasingly uncertain. It was a malaise that fed on itself. The more distortions the Government produced, the more it had to produce. The more it subsidized, the more it had to subsidize. The more it regulated, the more it had to regulate. The more it spent, the more it was given to spend, in an unceasing spiral that was making our industry inefficient and non-competitive and undermining our prospects for economic prosperity.
Mr. Speaker, Canadians know perfectly well, and it doesn't take a degree in economics to realize, that it doesn't really pay to get a subsidy of $1,000 if the subsidy has to generate $1,500 in taxes for the same year. Taxpayers know their arithmetic, and that is why in the last election they did not ask the Liberals to help them out of the economic mess we were in. When it came to power, the Government was firmly resolved to put an end to these destructive policies.
We made a clear statement of our objectives in November 1984 in our agenda for economic renewal. And now, two years later, we have made substantial progress in achieving these objectives. The results are eloquent proof that good management pays.
Mr. Speaker, good management means good government, and good government means that a government, instead of being part of the economic problem, starts solving that problem. At this point, perhaps 1 could illustrate the Government's emphasis on controlling operating and administration costs, always with a view to bringing down the deficit. Just to indicate how effective the Government's measures have been, in 1987-88, net operating costs will be essentially the same as in 1984-85. Now that, Mr. Speaker, is good management.
By reducing the deficit, which is not an end in itself, we increase employment, stimulate economic growth and expand the opportunities available for all Canadian men and women. The results are impressive. Since our Government came to power, the Canadian economy has produced 675,000 new jobs, because we created an economic climate favourable to economic growth and job creation. This record number of new jobs represents, for Quebec alone, 163,000 jobs created in less than 30 months, whereas the Liberals took 55 months to create 40,000 jobs. Since we first came into office we have therefore created four times as many jobs a month as did the Liberals. These are the figures which our forgetful colleagues opposite are trying to hide from the people. But I am confident, Mr. Speaker. And if one of the provinces so proudly displays the motto "Je me souviens", it is to remind members opposite that it was not born yesterday.
In addition, inflation has levelled at around 4 per cent. Real growth in the economy has averaged out at about 3.5 per cent,
a better achievement than that of the United States, second only to Japan among major industrialized nations. Interest rates have never been so low in almost ten years. Canadians would never have been able to enjoy such economic prosperity had the Conservatives not been at the helm. What this means is that a $50,000 five-year mortgage now costs $1,500 less a year than in 1984, a saving of about $125 a month. We are rightfully proud of these results, for they show that the less the Government interferes and the more it acts as an economic lever, the better private sector interests can achieve the goals they have set for themselves.
For instance, before we took office my riding, like so many others in Quebec, was in the doldrums. Unemployment was at an all-time high, prospects for improvement were dim, and the few small businesses which managed to survive were finally forced to close down after years of sustained efforts because nothing had been provided to help them. Thousands of new businesses have opened their doors and created new jobs, a fact which reflects growing confidence among both Canadians and foreigners alike. People know that Canada is again open for business. Statistics attest to that. Our national debt is a mortgage on future generations and we are successfully getting a handle on it. In terms of the economy, the deficit has dropped from 7.4 per cent a year when we took over to 5.1 per cent this year. Where it used to represent one and a half times the American deficit, on a proportional basis, both are now practically the same.
These are no longer projections or promises but facts, Mr. Speaker, and the world community has acknowledged that these results are the best posted by an industrialized nation. In addition, they were achieved without losing sight of our sense of responsibility and discernment.
Sixty-three per cent of our declining deficit with respect to the Gross National Product can be traced back to lower expenditures and sound management, but too often our friends opposite would rather forget that.
Rather than seeking only public political popularity and playing to the gallery, our Government preferred to emphasize good management even though this approach may antagonize some people. When we took over we decided to act responsibly and learn to live within our means. The Speech from the Throne delivered last October made it clear what the priorities of the Government would be in this parliamentary session and, within the constraints of our financial plan, they will be implemented over the coming months.
Unlike the previous Government, we have shown we can set our priorities and responsibly allot our resources to achieve these objectives. We have increased the agricultural gas tax rebate, something which the Hon. Member for Winnipeg- Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) conveniently forgot to mention earlier today. Finally, we have implemented a $1 billion special assistance program for Canadian grain producers. Moreover, we have done so without exceeding the expenditure objectives set in the 1986 budget.
March 3, 1987

There are hundreds of farmers in my constituency, so I find these measures particularly interesting and important. They are not aimed at helping small groups, but major sectors which are often put at a disadvantage. We shall pursue this disciplined and responsible action within the limits of the financial framework outlined in the budget.
The new refundable sales tax credit implemented in 1986 will provide assistance to lower income Canadians. We have also improved the child tax credit and developed a new benefit system to allow the neediest taxpayers to obtain prepayment of the credit each November.
A complete reform of pension mechanisms will promote retirement savings while improving pensions for all Canadians. Part-time workers and women will benefit particularly from the changes in pension standards.
As far as new initiatives are concerned, this budget represents a pause before we introduce our comprehensive tax reform proposals this spring. Mr. Speaker, we are continuing to work at the initiatives announced in the Speech from the Throne, including tax reform, and I know that you will find our proposals consistent with our program and good for Canada. Indeed, we have already initiated the reform process by introducing a minimum tax for high income Canadians. 1 wish to emphasize that we, the Conservatives, were the ones to introduce this tax.
Even my socialist friends opposite lacked the wisdom to support it, on the grounds that Bill C-23 was not strong enough. But the fact remains that the NDP, that third party, that champion of the widow and the orphan, has refused to support a minimum income tax provision for the rich.
We have gone a long way these last two and a half years. This budget shows our economic renewal program is bearing fruit and remains effective. We are on the right track. We must go on building a stronger, more aggressive, more flexible economy, for the benefit of every Canadian.

speechtext: I have a question for the Hon. Member. 1 listened to him earlier as he praised the favourable repercussions of the budget, and I would like him to state where he thinks his Government will get the money for women-targeted programs, especially child care? Where is that money in the budget?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for Outremont (Mrs. Pepin) for her excellent question. She listened to one part of my speech, as she just indicated. As you know, Mr. Speaker, when we came into office in 1984, we took over a business whose economic vehicles had nothing but flat tires. We had to repair several of them and change others, within our means. So, if this can reassure the Hon. Member for Outremont, she probably had an opportunity last night to see our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) before a women's group. He repeated that child care would be a priority for this Government. But as I said earlier, you know what little flexibility we had in reducing the
The Budget-Mr. Clement Cote
deficit. And the results, as I described them, are ample proof that Canadians made the right choice in 1984.
We remain convinced that as soon as the Liberals have finished digging into what I would like to call-and if my language is unparliamentary Mr. Speaker, you will certainly call me to order-I mean, into sceptic tanks, they will return to a somewhat more reasonable policy and will think more about Canadian men and women, including mothers-I say that to please the Hon. Member for Outremont-who need a more adequate child care system, as she had clearly demonstrated and as was previously stated. As soon as they realize the economic reality of this country, I am convinced that Canadian men and women will maintain these Hon. Members and this Government in their positions, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext: The Hon. Member for Outremont (Mrs. Pepin) on a supplementary question.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I should like to reply to my Hon. Conservative friend and ask him to explain to me why Canadian women were right to support a Government such as his. I should like to know also, because we are talking about the economic contribution of all Canadians, why we are not mentioning the significant contribution of Canadian women to the Canadian economy. When dealing with the overall impact of a budget, this is an aspect which we may have overlooked. 1 simply want to give him another opportunity to say what Canadian women have contributed to the economy and why they were right to support his government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think that the question itself provides the answer. Why were Canadians, particularly women, right to get rid of the former Government and have confidence in ours? Quite simply because the former Government was not leading them anywhere but towards a deficit and out-of-control indebtedness.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Tell me about women. You have cut several programs.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: As much as men, Mr. Speaker, women were aware of this unbearable situation, and why? Because they simply could no longer have confidence in them.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
1 must say that I listened very carefully to the excellent speech made by the Hon. Member, certainly more so in form than in substance. I can see the speech was very well prepared, but I must admit that I am less enthusiastic about the answers to the questions. These must be made directly and off the cuff, and the Hon. Member attempted to lower the debate by suggesting that Liberal Members ought to be less concerned about septic tanks. That gave me a clear idea of where he wanted to drag us.
The only question I have for him is that, first he did not answer the questions asked by my colleague from Outremont (Mrs. Pepin) concerning all those cut-backs in retraining centres and so on. She expressed her own views. I would like to ask the Hon. Member who again made a speech that was very

March 3, 1987
The Budget-Mr. Ernie Epp
well prepared-1 don't agree with the substance but I certainly admire the form, and you can tell there must be something new going around, when we have all these polished speeches, and we all know how the system operates in the House-but in any case, I would like to ask the Hon. Member whether he thought it was really necessary to have a budget at this time, since aside from a few additional taxes, the budget contains absolutely nothing. Couldn't this have been done in the form of a statement by the Minister, leaving the real budget until later this spring? Now we have to waste six full days on a Budget Speech we cannot really consider as such. Would the Hon. Member care to explain why he thinks it was really necessary to have a budget at this time?
Mir. Cote (Lac-Saint-Jean): Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the Hon. Member for his good words about the style and preparation of my speech. I would like to take this opportunity to give him a few words of encouragement, and his party as well, since as he said just now, he knows how the system operates. Since that is the case, and the Hon. Member has been able to see for himself that in addition to having good speeches, we can also have good policies and a good program and act on that program, I would urge the Hon. Member to get his colleagues and his leader to use the same system to give us a good set of alternative policies that is, if they have any, because they have been doing nothing but criticize.
To get back to the kind of answers I gave, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that my answers were as good as the questions, which means that the quality of the answers was in direct proportion to the quality of the questions.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to take part in the debate on the Budget presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) on February 18. The Budget presented that day was a sorry disappointment. One cannot, in debating it, but speak critically of what the Government put before us and speak with regret at the opportunities which are being lost.
The Minister of Finance spoke of the Budget from the standpoint of new initiatives, as representing a breathing space. 1 am far from the only person in the country who saw the Budget as a "do-nothing" Budget, as a Budget of lost opportunities, as a failure to recognize that there still were very serious problems facing Canadians in many regions of the country. The Minister of Finance was prepared to allow the forces that have favoured him up to this point to carry the country onward, in the hope that there would be a continuing gradual improvement of the sort which some regions of Canada have known.
Being realistic about the situation, I recognize that there has been one very happy feature of the situation over the last few years, though it is not a feature for which I think the Government deserves any credit at all. I am referring to the fact that
interest rates have fallen from the incredible levels which we knew in the early 1980s. Interest rates were at outrageous levels at the time, thanks to international action, chiefly by the Federal Reserve Board of the United States, which drove interest rates beyond 20 per cent and taught us all a useful lesson. If people thought before then that we could no longer have a depression, we all know these days that if we maintained interest rates at that point for a year or 18 months the globe would in fact experience a depression. There is no assurance these days that we are out of the woods at all as far as that is concerned.
The action taken by the Brazilian Government just last week in indicating a three-month moratorium on interest payments to the large banks which have lent so much to that country was an indication of how deeply we are still in the morass. However, I recognize that interest rates in Canada have fallen to more sensible levels, thanks to the good sense which has prevailed in other countries. As a result we have seen an increase in housing which has had the usual effect upon unemployment, with construction workers happily employed, paying taxes and no longer requiring unemployment insurance. That has represented some improvement in the economic situation.
In Thunder Bay in the last couple of weeks we have had the problem of variable entrance requirements being affected by some decline in interest rates resulting in people previously eligible for unemployment insurance at 10 weeks finding themselves out of luck because 16 weeks is now the requirement. In northwestern Ontario that seems to be a highly ironic thing to do at a time of still significant levels of unemployment above 10 per cent, and at a time when it is difficult to get work in the depths of winter. That kind of action should not be taken. It reflects the kinds of policies the Government carries on which were inherited from the previous Government and which the Conservative Government has done nothing at all to improve. I am speaking particularly of the variable entrance requirements which were designed to reduce the draw on the unemployment insurance fund in the late 1970s, but produced hardship for many Canadians.
The fact remains if there has been some improvement in a few places, but in many parts of Canada there remains much to be done. If we consider the unemployment insurance figures as they existed in January of this year we find Ontario's rate generally is set at 6.6 per cent. I have already indicated that we in northwestern Ontario are looking at 10 per cent plus. That is one indication, within a large province, of regional disparity.
Let us look at some of the other provinces. In British Columbia the unemployment rate is 13.6 per cent, on the Prairies, 9.4 per cent, Quebec, 10.8 per cent and in Atlantic Canada, 15.3 per cent. That was not a situation on which a Finance Minister should have been resting on his oars.
March 3, 1987

The Finance Minister does not just rest on his oars in these budgets, he socks it to Canadians in the way of increased taxation. We got some of it in this Budget. The decision to lay still more taxes on Canadians should provoke an outcry, a tax revolt, and I think it will as we approach the next election when Canadians recognize what is being done to them.
The Toronto Star published a story which appeared in Quorum yesterday. The figures it provides are fascinating. The Executive Director of the Social Planning Council in Toronto, Mr. Pennington points to two studies. The one noted at greater length is the one provided by the National Council on Welfare. As it happens the Fraser Institute in Vancouver, a very conservative think tank, has been providing figures that fit right in. What does Mr. Pennington tell us:
-he was astonished to learn that two such radically different groups as the National Council on Welfare and the Fraser Institute-reached the same conclusion in studies released last month.
The studies show that individual Canadians face federal tax bills in the next fiscal year that will be 48 per cent higher than those they paid in 1984-85-
That is, when the Government obtained its mandate.
-while corporations will face only a 4.3 per cent increase over the same period.
And they show that an urban family of four living on the poverty line with a $20,812 annual income faces a 35 per cent tax hike over what they paid in 1985, while a couple earning $100,000 will see only a 2 per cent increase.
That is fairness in taxation from a Conservative Government, Mr. Speaker? The article goes on:
The National Welfare Council study shows that a two-income family of four, earning a total of $ 15,000,-
Clearly below the poverty line.
-faces a 90 per cent increase over what they paid in 1985.
"I'm jolted," said Barb Couchman, Executive Director of the Family Services Association-
I would think that Conservative back-benchers might also feel jolted by what their colleague, the Minister of Finance has done to the Canadian people. What we have here is the most rank unfairness in taxation, laying the burden of Government on the people. It is fine to talk about assisting those most in need, as the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) likes to do, but after you lay taxes like this on Canadians, on the poor, it will be very, very difficult to recover.
The result of these actions, which for the average Canadian family of four means a tax increase since the Government came into office of about $1,380, has had one very important economic effect. It transfers money to the Government which the people of Canada should have to spend at a time of high unemployment in most of the country and at a time of very real need to support economic activity, production and sales. Because disposable income has been lost to Canadians, demand has been very weak.
Economic depression begins to affect other parts of the country other than the resource industries which have been battered in case after case. Just look at the mining, the oil and gas and the farming sectors which are disaster areas of the
The Budget-Mr. Ernie Epp
Canadian economy. This is an important reason why unemployment rates are at the present level, that they are and yet we have a Minister of Finance refusing to recognize it. Sure, he says in the Budget speech, the benefits of our strong economic performance have not been evenly shared across the country. Some regions are hurting. My God, most of the regions of Canada are hurting, Mr. Speaker. Only southern Ontario has anything to be very happy about in these circumstances. Of course, a Finance Minister from Bay Street may be quite content with that, but most Canadians are not, and it is a situation with which the Minister of Finance has refused to come to grips.
In the area of regional disparity spending, about which the Minister should be doing something, he has reduced spending significantly. Three years ago the regional development spending totalled $14.85 billion. By the coming fiscal year that will have dropped almost $3 billion to $11.95 billion. With that kind of decline of over one-fifth, it is not surprising that very little happens in the various regions of Canada.
I want to focus on one particular aspect of the Minister's taxation principles to underscore how he is refusing to take opportunities to improve the situation of the Canadian people and create employment. This Minister of Finance in his very first Budget reduced the capital gains tax for those who are lucky enough to have the money to get in on it. This was a $500,000 tax holiday. That tax holiday was interesting to some people but, of course, Canadians who have $15,000 or $20,000 in annual income will not be able to make use of it. In the same Toronto Star report to which I have referred we are told people are spending $12,000 of their annual income in Toronto just covering rent. People like that will not be able to take advantage of that $500,000 capital gains tax holiday. The Minister of Finance thinks he is going to lose $850 million this coming year in taxes as a result. That is very interesting, Mr. Speaker, because he admits the loss.
The Government talks about child care. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) yesterday was promising again that there would be some activity in this area. If the Finance Minister had not given this money away and instead spent less than one-half of it, namely, $320 million on improved child care he would have helped all those middle-income families who desperately need it. At the moment they are forced to spend their own hard-earned money, which they would like to put to other uses, ensuring that their children are properly cared for. This would have provided about 25,000 additional spaces for children and could well have created 5,000 jobs. There is money which the Minister of Finance could have taken in, which may not create a single job in Canada. But, after all, one can have condominiums in Florida or other places, buy art works or deal in antiques or whatever.
There is no assurance of any improvement in employment. The Minister of Finance passed up a splendid opportunity to create additional employment. That failure is a splendid

March 3, 1987
The Budget-Mr. Stackhouse
example of the short-sightedness of the Minister and his Government in giving away money to the wealthy, taxing corporations only a little bit more, while socking the poor and middle-income earner with an incredible burden.
As a Member of Parliament from northwestern Ontario, I want to address the issue of regional development. I have already made reference to the decline in total spending on regional development from almost $15 billion three years ago to under $12 billion today. That points out that there is less concern about regions today, although Lord knows it was bad enough before that Government was elected.
When the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion was considering the assistance it might provide, we in Thunder Bay found ourselves in the odd position of being lumped in with the City of Toronto. I suppose it is nice to be included in the prosperous half of the country statistically, but the people in my region do not think of it as having anything like the economic strength which characterizes the area known as The Golden Horseshoe, where Asian companies are building automobile assembly plants these days. We just do not have the resources or attractiveness of southern Ontario. Yet the staff at our DRIE office has been cut back and there is precious little taking place in the way of regional development.
There were of course other programs and the Government, by reducing spending, has damaged regional development in that way as well. I can cite several examples. When I visited the Canadian Forestry Service Centre in Sault Ste. Marie last fall I was told that reforestation spending through the Canada Employment Commission was being cut and likely to disappear entirely. The Government is proud of the Canadian Jobs Strategy. I am sorry to say that in our region there is concern among those who are trying to assist women in obtaining training because the Canadian Jobs Strategy has weakened those programs almost fatally.
Another example is that of our local advisory council. We considered Challenge '87, another program the Government is proud of. Quite frankly, I found it shameful that in the third season of a summer employment experience development program organized by the Government the situation of deadlines, late release of application forms, and so on, was just about as bad as it was the first year. I could understand it happening in the first year when changes were being made in order to produce a better plan. However, it seems to me completely shameful that this continues in 1987. In particular,
I cannot understand how the Government can do this to the private sector, the small businesses it wants to take part in the program. It is simply not fair to give people just a couple of weeks to come up with projects, fill in and file the applications. It is most certainly not fair to students to receive approval as late as the middle of April, and only then be able to hire other students.
Those are only some of the shortcomings of the Government in regional development. We very badly need the Government to recognize the action it needs to take. We need to recognize that resources have to be provided. I have watched the
Government fail in its efforts at co-operative development for months now. It has worked quietly, we are told, on a response to the task force on co-operative development. We still have not had any public statement. Here we have a report which has been before the Government from the beginning of its mandate and there has not been a response.
As well, we in the NDP are very critical of an economy which is shot full of government incentives. However, I can understand the co-operative financial institutions, such as credit unions, seeking something of the same sort for themselves. Yet again the Minister of Finance has refused to do anything. Here is a potential for community-based economic development to be encouraged, yet the Government has blown it entirely. It is playing around with things like community futures committees. However, I do not see any substantial assistance or support for community-based development. People talk about potential for some special kind of training. I expect there will be consideration of relocation in some communities. However, there will not be the kind of financial assistance which is not seen as a subsidy. The Minister of Finance always thinks in terms of subsidies but it ought to be seen as an investment in the community. The Government is incapable of seeing things that way, and that is why it will be turfed out in the next election, and why the people of Canada are going to turn to the NDP which wants to encourage community-based economic development in order to produce prosperity and employment from coast to coast.

speechtext: Questions or comments. Debate.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks in this budget debate will focus on the announcement by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) that we can soon expect major reform of the income tax system. He certainly deserves the congratulations of every Member of this House for having the vision, courage and foresight to see that the jerry-built, ramshackle, out-moded system he and the rest of us inherited can soon be replaced by a rational, planned, contemporary system.
In his budget address the Minister committed himself to reform which would reduce income tax rates, achieve greater equity for taxpayers, and inspire economic growth. In my remarks I want to focus on one reform which can contribute to all those objectives. For half a century income tax has been administered as a kind of legal larceny. I say that without reflection on the integrity of any Minister or public servant. They have all operated within the law. The fault lies with the law itself and what it has legitimized. It lies with a system which has permitted Governments to reach in the pockets of all income taxpayers and seize what has rightfully belonged to them for themselves.
I make that claim on a premise that a democracy should not make the assumptions of a totalitarian state. By that I refer to the opinion advanced half a century ago by Harold Joseph
March 3, 1987

Laski who wrote that in the 20th century governments have extended their power over more and more of life to a point where governments assume that they have a right to control all of it and should they refrain from controlling some area, it is because they have chosen to refrain. At no point does a government today, Laski suggested, recognize that it has no right to extend its control over that area.
My remarks are based on the conviction that a democracy does not make that assumption as a totalitarian government does, that in a democracy there are recognized limits to the legitimate authority of governments, that there are areas of life which belong to people on their own without intrusion by government. I ask the House today to focus on what that belief can mean for tax reform.
I submit that it means that governments will respect that a person has a responsibility to provide for himself and his dependents and, consequently, has a right to the income required to fulfil that responsibility. My thesis is that a person has what can be regarded as a human right to the income required to fulfil the natural responsibility to support oneself and one's dependants.
If we agree on that principle, I ask the House to go one step more with me and agree that persons should have that basic income free from tax. It should be respected as the person's basic income and should, therefore, be free from any trespass by a government.
I recognize that some Members might see that as a radically innovative and radically unpractical point of view. However, I submit it has already been recognized in principle by the personal exemption granted taxpayers, spouses and dependants. I am aware that many understand such exemptions simply as being tax deductions, that is tax avoidance provisions which governments have allowed and which governments can take away. However, I am arguing that that is precisely what they are not. They are essentially different from what are called deductions, should not be considered tax avoidance, and should not be subject to the changes and chances of government policy.
The term "exemption" itself suggests another meaning. It can mean that part of a person's income is respected as rightly exempt or free from taxation because it is income which the person needs to fulfil this natural responsibility to provide for himself and his dependants. I submit that income tax should be collected only on the surplus income, that being surplus in the sense of being what remains after a person has earned and retained what is needed for human existence.
If that can be recognized, or at least implied, in the present tax system, why speak of it today? I have two reasons. One is that the current exemption is too small to meet the need. The other is that as small as the exemption is there are those who want to take it away. The present exemption can be defended if it is no more than an arbitrary figure chosen to give the taxpayer another way of reducing taxable income. It is, however, indefensible if the exemption means that the tax
The Budget-Mr. Stackhouse
collector respects this natural right to a basic income free from the tax collector's eager grasp. The current exemption would not provide for the existence of any human in today's Canada. It does not even keep pace with inflation. The 1986 exemption, for example, was $4,180, up only $40 over the previous year, even though that meant an increase of less than 1 per cent to cope with inflation of 4 per cent.
Canadians need a personal exemption which more approximates what they need for basic human existence; not for luxury, not for comfort, not even for security, just for existence. I submit that that amount should be seen as exempt from the tax collector. It should be respected as the natural right of the person, upon which the Government has no right to intrude. I would like to think that tax reform would bring us a system in which we might conceive of an invisible sign on an invisible fence around a very visible income. The sign would read, "Personal, Private, Tax Collectors Keep Out". This belongs to the person as a natural right for his natural existence.
I said that there are those who would eliminate this personal exemption, small and inadequate as it is. I understand the motives and respect the arguments. One argument is that the exemption offers more tax benefit to the middle and upper income earners than it does to the lower income earners. With respect, I can argue that that critique shows that such persons insist on equating the personal exemption with any other deduction and with any other tax avoidance provision. I ask them to see that the exemption respects that all of us, regardless of income level, have a common humanity for which each of us must provide. We all have a common humanity which requires each of us to accept the responsibility to provide for our own existence and those who depend on us. Therefore, each of us should have a basic income which is exempt from taxation.
1 recognize, as does every Member of this House, that low income persons and families need assistance which others do not. Justice demands that they receive it. However, I submit that the income tax system is not the way to provide it. That system should be seen for what it is, a method of raising revenue. It should not be a program for redistributing the wealth. The strong should assist the weak, but the income tax system is not the way to do it. That should be the work of the Department of National Health and Welfare, not the work of the Department of Finance.
I therefore urge that the forthcoming income tax reform retain personal exemptions and make them adequate to meet a rising cost of living. We ought to take very seriously the great pressure on individuals and families, certainly in large cities such as Scarborough from which I come, to cope with the rising cost of living, so frequently on limited resources. An individual trying to be self-supporting on $12,000 a year today is a person who is struggling. A family of four trying to maintain themselves on an income of $20,000 a year today is certainly struggling. We must ask ourselves whether the income tax system should put another burden upon those

March 3, 1987
The Budget-Mr. Stackhouse
people. Should we demand of them yet another challenge to be faced? Can we think in terms of lifting at least some of that burden, removing some of that challenge, so that they can have the dignity of self support, the self worth of maintaining themselves without the country making that almost impossible for them?
I recognize that whenever we talk about raising exemptions or improving benefits we are talking about either a loss of revenue or an increase of government expenditure. We must address ourselves to the question of how to meet the need. The fact is that although there is an amazingly large number of Canadians earning $12,000 a year or less, the amount of tax revenue coming out of that large number is proportionately small, about $650 million. The number of individuals and families coping with the cost of living on incomes of $20,000 or less is larger and the tax burden is correspondingly larger. It is about $4.5 billion. We are now beginning to talk about big money.
As we contemplate the forthcoming tax reform we must keep in mind the possibility and, indeed, the absolute requirement that the corporate sector contribute a much more just and rational portion of the income tax revenue of the Government. It is shocking to read the report entitled "Road Map to Tax Reform" issued by the Economic Council of Canada and to learn, according to this document, that the corporate income tax is riddled with a variety of tax credits, allowances and deductions. In any recent year, about one-half of all corporations paid no tax at all. In some cases, the report states, this was because the corporation had experienced real losses. We must not fly with flights of fancy to think that all the needs of the country can be made up from the corporate sector, but the report goes on to say that in other cases the fact they paid no tax was due to the provision of the corporate income tax legislation and to the competence of the accountants and legal experts.
When we are talking about a corporate sector which pays income tax just under $10 billion and we learn that that represents taxation paid by no more than half the corporations of this country, we see that one dimension that our forthcoming income tax reform must explore is the possibility of a more rational and more just contribution by that sector to the life and well-being of this country.
I submit that by that reform, along with others, it will be possible to give some further respect to individuals and families who are trying to cope with their natural responsibility to support themselves and their dependants on very limited incomes. I submit that for years they have been unjustly, irrationally, and unnecessarily forced to suffer further by the Government intruding upon that which should be regarded as theirs.
What I have described today can be called tax reform from below, in contrast to what I will label tax reform from above. The kind of tax reform that we read about in the United States
can be fairly described as tax reform from above, for one of its priorities has been the reduction of income tax brackets, and the reduction of income tax rates very often at the top level of income. There is an argument to be said in favour of that, but I would plead for some further recognition in this country for a tax reform that will do justice to those who are striving to meet the challenge of human existence with limited resources.
I would plead that this Parliament, in undertaking this historic reform which can be before us within the next few months, will give a priority to tax reform from below and that we will try for a tax reform that will bring justice from the bottom up, rather than privilege from the top down. That alone will satisfy the demands of democracy.
The reason I have asked for the attention of the House today is that, more than anything else, a tax system expresses the values of a society and expresses the real principles upon which a society is based. We can see in the kind of tax reform to which I have referred the opportunity for a democratic system such as Canada has not enjoyed for many days.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am always interested in listening to a radical in the Conservative ranks discussing what might be the best of all possible worlds, but not of course, as it is made by the present Minister of Finance. The Hon. Member referred to a tax system as a means of expressing the values of a society. Will he clearly characterize the values that prevail in the Budget of the Minister of Finance who increases taxation on the poor so sharply while guarding the corporations? In light of the Hon. Member's vision of society, it is strange that one can have such a sound and democratic vision which has not been achieved by the Government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for this opportunity to extol further the merits of the Budget and the virtues of the Minister who presented it. Let me add a few ways in which the needs of lower income people have been met by the Government and this Budget.
When we took office, one of the problems which confronted many Members, including myself, was the spectre of widespread unemployment. In the community I represent, I find more frequently that there are signs saying "Help Wanted".

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is Toronto.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Hon. Member says Toronto. I remind the spokesman for the NDP that Toronto is part of Canada and I am shocked that the NDP is not aware of that.
A second way in which the Government and its Minister of Finance have contributed to the well-being of ordinary Canadians has been by slashing interest rates. It has been decades since we have seen such a home building boom in this country as we have witnessed in recent years. This is primarily because of the lower interest rate policy.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He is building a new house.
March 3, 1987

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I congratulate him. He will know what Government to credit for it. These are indications of the way in which our Government is progressive and conservative at the same time. We are progressive in opening opportunities for people as a way of conserving the fundamental values upon which this country is based.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member made a very good point about trying to have an effective layer of tax exempt income which would be very much higher than the basic $4,000 that exists now. He also suggested that this layer could be as high as $12,000.
However, if there was a $12,000 tax exemption, over three-quarters of the benefit would flow to the very highest income Canadians. Does he not believe that a better way to proceed would be to have a tax credit so that the tax paid by the first $12,000 for someone who is earning $12,000 would be refunded or credited to them, rather than increasing the exemption, so that the money went to the people who need it most?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank my friend and neighbour for this significant question. It gives us an opportunity for an all too brief debate on the issue raised in my remarks and in his question. It is a fundamental issue which requires more debate than we can afford today, and I hope we can return to it.
We are not talking only about benefiting the low-income person. We are talking about respecting the right of every human being to a basic income to meet the needs of a human existence, which the middle-income person has and the upper-income person has. We are saying that each of us, having a common humanity, has a need for a basic income which is common to us all. That is the first point.
Second, if we had a larger exemption similar to what I have described we would be able to totally remove many people from the income tax rolls who are now on those rolls. Some of the income they are now paying to the Government would be returned to them.
Third, many people who are unable to cope with their needs because of low income or family responsibilities, regardless of how they manage their income, require some supplementation by society. I do not see the income tax system as a way of doing that. I would rather see that coming through forms of payment which Parliament would authorize and the Government would administer. That is my approach to the issue. I recognize that the Hon. Member has raised a valid and important question and I hope he and I can debate it again at a later time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have both a comment and a question. First, I commend the Hon. Member for Scarborough West (Mr. Stackhouse) for the positive mention in The Toronto Star this morning. I think it shows he is a dogged
The Budget-Mr. Stackhouse

speechtext:
That is no problem at all in terms of credit cards and interest rates, so we can do a trade off here. The Hon. Member mentioned that some Members of the New Democratic Party do not realize Toronto is part of Canada. Toronto has done very well. In fact, about 90 per cent of the jobs created in this country in the last year have been in Toronto, primarily because of the auto industry. Does the Hon. Member have some ideas on how we can spread some of that affluence across the country? I look at western Canada and I see tremendously high unemployment rates. I see Albertans who are very discouraged about what is happening. I look at northern Ontario and see an unemployment rate around 15 per cent. In some places in Atlantic Canada unemployment rates are as high as 20 per cent.
I look at western Canada in terms of the farm economy and find that our farmers are receiving prices now which in some cases are worse than they received in the 1930s. Even with the $1 billion deficiency payment, the maximum price a farmer can now receive for his bushel of wheat is $3.50. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight) knows well of what 1 speak because he is a farmer in western Canada. The deficiency payment is 48 cents a bushel and the maximum price is $3.50 for a bushel of wheat for the Canadian farmer. The American farmer meanwhile, because of subsidies, receives a minimum of $4.80 U.S., which is about $6 Canadian.
What do we do to spread some of this wealth around? I am very happy for Toronto. Toronto is very much part of Canada. We are not all Torontonians and we all deserve to receive a fair shake. The Hon. Member did say that there should be a minimum amount of Government. I am paraphrasing him, but he said that sometimes there is too much government. However, is it not one of the roles of Government to try to divide more equally the national pie so that the Saskatchewan farmer and the Newfoundland cod fisherman can receive a more fair share? I wonder if I have the support of the Hon. Member opposite to help us in this very worthy cause of getting more money into regional development, more money for people like fishermen and farmers in order to give them a better chance to be competitive in terms of having a fair share of the national pie? We do not all want to be Torontonians, but we all want the same opportunity which Torontonians now have. We all want to ensure that there are jobs for people regardless of whether they live in Toronto, Yorkton, St. John's, or even Calgary, where my friend to my left knows there is considerable unrest because of growing unemployment.

subsubtopic: PRESERVATION OF SOUTH MORESBY-PRIME MINISTER'S FORTHCOMING MEETING WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA PREMIER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in exactly two days the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) will meet with
Premier Vander Zalm while loggers are beginning to cut timber in Windy Bay on Lyell Island. This is a unique forest ecosystem with beautiful spruce and cedar trees, the streams are filled with salmon and trout, and the sky is criss-crossed by all kinds of birds.
Canadians from coast to coast recognize the immense value of the South Moresby archipelago, and of Lyell Island in particular, and want this heritage protected for the enjoyment of this and future generations. We urge the Prime Minister to impress on Premier Vander Zalm that the preservation of South Moresby is of national and international importance. The Prime Minister should ask the Premier to stop the logging, avoid further confrontation between the Haida Nation and the loggers, and negotiate a national park that would cover only 0.2 per cent of B.C.'s forests. This is the kind of leadership Canadians expect from their Prime Minister.

subtopic: SYSTEM TO MONITOR SPOUSES DEFAULTING ON SUPPORT PAYMENTS
SYSTEM TO MONITOR SPOUSES DEFAULTING ON SUPPORT PAYMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 60 per cent of single-parent families headed by women live in poverty. This is not only the result of low incomes earned by female family heads, but also because enforcement orders are often not enforced. Poor single parents and their children often receive no support from the other financially secure parent.
The Family Orders Enforcement Assistance Act which the Government passed in June, 1986, will allow the attachment of moneys under federal jurisdiction. Yesterday's Estimates gave Revenue Canada $627,000 to implement a computer system to nab spouses who are defaulting on support payments. Their refunds will be withheld until they meet their support obligations. Some 30,000 Canadians who last year ripped off their spouses, their families and their children, will find that this callous disregard for their families will not go unchecked. The Government intends to ensure that they live up to their obligations.

maintopic: FUNDING OF AIDS DISEASE RESEARCH AND EDUCATION
FUNDING OF AIDS DISEASE RESEARCH AND EDUCATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recent reports have stated that an estimated 1,200 people in Edmonton are infected with the deadly AIDS virus. AIDS is spreading at such an alarmingly rapid rate in Canada that it is time for all Canadians to become serious about AIDS education. Our Government has scheduled an AIDS education program to begin this March and has pledged $3.7 million toward that goal. This is only part of a total of $39 million for AIDS research and education.
We must all accept the reality of AIDS in our society and educate all Canadians, both young and old, on the far-reaching effects of this disease. We should support full public information in the communities, in the school systems and through the media. It is only through such measures that we will be able to combat this disease in a realistic manner.
I commend the Department of National Health and Welfare for its commitment of funds and its dedication to conquering this plague.

subtopic: SELECTION OF BRANCH LINES FOR REHABILITATION ON PRAIRIES
SELECTION OF BRANCH LINES FOR REHABILITATION ON PRAIRIES
speechtext:

March 3, 1987

subtopic: GOVERNMENT MEASURES TO IMPROVE POSITION OF WOMEN
GOVERNMENT MEASURES TO IMPROVE POSITION OF WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the First Ministers' Conference last November, the Prime Minister tabled "Dimensions of Equality: A Federal Government Work Plan for Women". This document specifies the measures our Government is undertaking to promote women's achievement of equality.
As we approach International Women's Day it is appropriate to review the many initiatives that our Government is pursuing to improve the status of women. These include work in the area of pensions, family violence, child care, women's health, sports and fitness, and issues related to women's employment. The Government is committed to addressing the particular needs of farm women, aboriginal women, disabled women, immigrant women, and visible minority women.
In short, we are determined to create the conditions that will enable all Canadian women to pursue their ambitions on an equal footing with men, and to realize their full potential in society.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday, the Main Estimates tabled by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) were one more indication that Quebec is being penalized by this Conservative Government.
Despite an unemployment rate of 11 per cent, Quebec has seen no change in the level of its transfer payments. Ontario, on the other hand, with an unemployment rate of 6.6 per cent, will receive $550 million more in transfer payments, an increase of 7 per cent. As for the social welfare component,
Quebec's share of transfer payments will go down 7.6 per cent, from $1.26 billion to $1.16 billion for this year.

It should come as no surprise today that the Progressive Conservative Party enjoys only 10 per cent of the public support among Quebec voters.
This morning, the newspaper La Presse contains an article on the Estimates, under a headline that speaks for itself: "Quebec feels the pinch".
Mr. Speaker, I urge all Conservative Members from Quebec to wake up and make sure their Conservative Government is giving Quebecers a fair deal.

Mr. Speaker, once again the federal Government has ignored the worsening state of our harbours and wharfs. The budget for small craft harbours is simply a drop in the bucket. Dependable and well maintained harbours and wharfs are absolutely essential.
The Government's neglect is a threat to the safety of Canadian fishermen and boaters. While the Government bails out banks and squeezes low and middle-income taxpayers for every last cent, the real needs of Canadians are ignored. In my own constituency fishermen in West Point, Tignish, Fishing Cove, and Alberton are kept waiting and waiting.
I urge the Government to fulfil its responsibilities and to allocate some badly needed assistance to our harbours and wharfs.
