subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When the House took recess at one o'clock, the Hon. Member for Saint-Henri-Westmount (Mr. Johnston) had the floor.

March 3, 1987
The Budget-Mr. Johnston

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this occasion to speak in the Budget debate. This is the first opportunity that I have had since the Minister delivered his quite extraordinary Budget. My reaction to the Budget was one of surprise. Perhaps one could even say astonishment or as we say in Quebec-

-I was speechless when 1 read the document.
I asked myself in the lock-up which preceded the delivery of the Budget why we needed to be locked up all afternoon to look at such a skimpy proposal. Why a Budget or, more important, why call the document delivered by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) a Budget?

Granted, they had to introduce a few taxes, and I will have a word to say about that this afternoon. He said it was necessary to reduce his deficit. I will have a word to say about that as well.

In a few moments 1 will come to the shameful exercise, how he attempted to get the deficit down. A simple statement by the Minister and a tabling of a Notice of Ways and Means in the House would have been sufficient. It would have been the appropriate thing to do, given the kinds of proposals the Minister brought to us that evening a week and a half ago.
Apart from the rhetoric in the document, which I think can be best described as self-congratulatory claptrap, what has the exercise we witnessed accomplished and what was it intended to accomplish? Was it simply to tell us once again, for the third time, that we would have tax reform in the future? Was that the purpose of the exercise? I will also have a word to say about tax reform.
I would admit-and I think most Hon. Members would agree-that the Minister by and large has enjoyed a reputation as a straightshooter, or perhaps as one of a few stars in a galaxy of black holes, or perhaps as a beacon of hope shining across a sea of incompetence if not corruption. 1 fear that with the Budget the Minister has set about to destroy that reputation by engaging in fiscal flimflam at best. He has allowed himself to be used as a decoy, probably to draw fire away from the flock of wild turkeys which surrounds him on the government benches.
Why has the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) done this to the Minister of Finance? Why has the Minister of Finance permitted this to be done to himself? 1 suspect that some public relations genius-perhaps Dalton Camp or probably Dalton Camp-saw a Budget, even a Budget totally devoid of substance, as a good diversionary tactic to get the Opposition and the media off the problems of scandals, incompetence, and
corruption which have plagued the Government. In fact, they have hobbled the Government and have brought the Government to the lowest level of public support or public esteem since Gallup began taking polls on popular support in 1942. Indeed that is a deserving mark of historic achievement.

But what a public relations disaster, Mr. Speaker. What is particularly clear from the speech by my hon. friend, the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau), who responded to the Minister's Budget speech, is the Government's and the Minister s record on the economy and especially on taxation. That is crystal clear.

Not only did the Minister act as a decoy, as I suggested, but he has quite properly added himself to that flock of turkeys and has become a prime target, and deservedly so. He is guilty of complicity in this public relations exercise scheme because he in fact did not have a bona fide Budget to deliver.
The Government simply rolled out the Minister to the centre of the national stage. He is their own Mr. Clean. They regard him as a white knight, a Sir Galahad, but he had nothing with which to defend himself. He had no Budget. He had no real proposals. His attire was skimpy and resembled more that of Lady Godiva than that of Sir Galahad. Like her, he has been totally exposed in the course of this exercise. For example, his budget documents show us in stark terms the failures of his policies to date.

To recall a few highlights of this record, Mr. Speaker, I suggest we look at the direct taxes paid by Canadian taxpayers since this Government came to power and since the present Minister of Finance was appointed.
1 am referring, Mr. Speaker, to the Minister's own "Budget papers". On page 21, we find table 3.6, "Budgetary Revenue Projections". We see that between 1984-85 and 1987-88, there was an increase of $14 billion in personal income tax collected under the Income Tax Act, an increase of 48 per cent. Shame!
If we look at sales and excise taxes and duties, which are also paid by Canadians, by individuals, by consumers and their families, all these taxes have increased from $14 billion to $22 billion, which means $7.5 billion more or an increase of 53 per cent.
However, despite these increases, this year's deficit, that is, the deficit for 1986-87, will be the same as at the end of 198384. What a record. I may remind you, Mr. Speaker, that 198384 was the last full year under this country's previous Liberal administration.

Next year the Minister can do no better. He is forecasting a deficit of $29.3 billion which is only $200 million less than he forecast last year for the current year. So much for the Minister's projections! More important-and this is where I say the Minister has engaged in fiscal flimflam or in a shell
March 3, 1987

game-he has achieved this reduction in a manner which, in my judgment, leaves his credibility in tatters. The single major revenue initiative found in the Budget is to require employers to remit twice monthly instead of once monthly the taxes which are held from employees.
The Minister calls this, accelerated remittances of source deductions. For me it is a transparent example of very creative bookkeeping. It creates a false impression and is intended to create a false indication of the true deficit position.
Let me explain, Mr. Speaker. This additional burden which is being imposed upon Canadian employers has the effect, in terms of the deficit, of moving one payroll date back from April of 1988 to March of 1988. That is estimated to bring an additional $1.2 billion into the 1987-1988 year. Of course, it removes $1.2 billion from the immediate following months in the 1988-1989 year. What kind of image of sound financial management does that project, Mr. Speaker? Does the Minister seriously think that borrowing from Paul in 1988-89 to pay Peter in 1987-88 fools anyone? Frankly, I regard it as an irresponsible manipulation of the Government's cash flows to meet a deficit objective. Imposing that additional paper burden, additional hardship and additional loss of interest on small Canadian businesses, municipalities and employers right across the country simply to meet an artificially established deficit objective is irresponsible, and I say shame! I expected much more from this Minister of Finance than that kind of fancy bookkeeping footwork. If he puts the amount where it should be, without this change and accelerated cash flow in 1988-89, the deficit becomes $30.5 billion.
I never thought that we would have to scrutinize the Minister's actions on issues of this kind. Previously I must admit I did see the Minister as a tinkerer in many respects. Now he has become "Wilson the accelerator". How far will he carry that acceleration, Mr. Speaker? Now that he has discovered this magic recipe to accelerate payments, can we count on him to limit the damage or are we going to find more distortions in future budgets? I hope we can count on the Minister to limit the distortion to this one exercise. Even then I say it is totally improper.
The Minister of Finance may have discovered a recipe and in future demand prepayment of future years taxes. Who knows? I understand that that practice has been followed in some other countries. Prepaying taxes for future years would quickly reduce the deficit but give a totally false perception and create a false reality in the country's financial condition.
I know that you suffered through the Budget speech yourself, Mr. Speaker. You know that it devoted a great deal of time to the issue of tax reform and what wonderful tax reform is planned. As I said, this is the third time we have been told about tax reform, which we have yet to see.
The Budget-Mr. Johnston

What is interesting, however, Mr. Speaker, is the fact that all his initiatives as Minister of Finance to this date and the tax increases which I have just mentioned are in direct conflict with the objective of the tax reform he is now proposing. Such a reform would be in conflict with the tax measures he has taken to date, including the most substantial increase of individual taxes in Canadian history. Now, the Minister wants to initiate a tax reform to correct his own mistakes. In his paper, he points out that the key to tax reform is to reduce the tax rate of individual taxpayers, even though he has just increased individual taxes for all Canadians.

Having created this extraordinary burden, this mess in terms of the fiscal system, not the least of which was the capital gains tax exemption which he stubbornly refuses to recognize is an error and should correct, he now seeks the way out of this dilemma through tax reform. This would be humorous I suppose if it were not so serious for Canadians.
Let me return to my point. There is no Budget here. There is no fiscal plan. How can one have a Budget in this country without a fiscal plan? It was the Royal Commission on Financial Management and Accountability, the so-called Lambert Commission report, that told Government that one should have a five-year fiscal plan. To give the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) credit, when he was Minister of Finance briefly, rightfully, back in 1979, one good thing he did was to include a five-year fiscal plan which was continued by the successive Liberal Government. This Government has refused to deliver a proper fiscal plan since it has been in office. It has delivered no fiscal plan at all, just simply projections for the next year. The public and parliamentarians are entitled to know what the fiscal plan is that the Government has in its own possession in the Department of Finance. We know that the information exists. We are entitled to see it and the Government should be obliged to give it to us.
If the Minister is not going to produce a fiscal plan, and if there is no more than this self congratulatory clap-trap that I have described, and there is no more than the imposition of a few taxes, again I say why a Budget? He did remove the ill-conceived taxes on Christmas trees.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And books.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
You will recall the tax we placed on ourselves, Mr. Speaker, to get back at the Americans for the tax they imposed on shakes and shingles. We told the Minister at the time that it was fiscal suicide by self-immolation. He did not agree. Finally the Minister has accepted our advice and has wisely withdrawn that tax. He did not do it with humility. He said the circumstances had changed. Of course, the circumstances have not changed at all and the other tax is still in place. He simply recognized the stupidity of his own actions and those of his Government, but he incorporated it in his speech as if it were some quite remarkable achievement that

March 3, 1987
The Budget-Mr. Johnston
had been brought about by the imposition of those taxes in the first instance.
Then the Minister puts a tax on airline tickets, Mr. Speaker, which hurts the regions of this country. The Minister tells us that that particular tax was recommended by his colleague, the Minister of Transport, which I thought was indeed remarkable. Nonetheless, again we have this marked insensitivity to the distant regions of Canada.
In that same vein, the Minister has imposed a fuel tax which once again, apart from the hardship on individuals and the increased tax at the pump, is a tax on distance. It hurts tourism, trucking and it hurts the consumer, especially the consumers in the regions. The tax has to be passed on. It has been passed on before and it will be passed on again. This is a direct tax on distance, a direct slap, as I say, at the regions.
In an address last fall in Toronto I noted the Minister stated that one of the difficulties in trying to match U.S. tax rates in Canada would be due to the higher cost in our economy as a result of geography and demographics. If he believed that, why would he simply turn around and again add to those costs in his Budget by putting a tax on transportation fuel?
We do need a Budget. We now need a real Budget, not this public relations exercise, not this self-congratulatory statement with taxes that are not neutral but harmful. We need a Budget that deals with the problems facing the country:

the environment, employment, the regions, senior citizens, women, housing, research and development, education, small businesses, transport and tourism. All those issues are forgotten in the budget recently tabled in this House.

Where is it? Where are the solutions to these problems? When will we see them? After this exercise that, as I say, we suffered through with great anticipation, and the media from all over the country gathered in Ottawa to listen to the great pronouncements from our Minister of Finance, I am not convinced that this Minister can deliver the goods with respect to this list of problems which I raised, this list of concerns which haunt Canadians in every walk of life from coast to coast, in every region, hamlet and village. These are the real problems. When is the Minister going to address them?

When is the Minister going to deliver? When will he address the real problems of Canadians? When will he give us something concrete about the tax reform, which is supposed to improve our tax system, to provide equity, to stimulate economic development, to encourage the regions and to protect the neediest members of our society? When are we going to have this tax reform?
Mr. Speaker, we in the Opposition are very disappointed at the performance of this minister. He has really ruined his reputation with his little game. He has played a dirty trick on
us.

speechtext:
Questions or comments. Debate. The Hon. Member for Bonavista-Trinity-Conception (Mr. Johnson).
Resuming debate with the Hon. Member for Bonavista- Trinity-Conception.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure to take part in this debate and support the third Budget my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), has produced. It is a Budget which clearly demonstrates that the Government has successfully met the challenge of maintaining a sound and steady management of both the fiscal and economic situation of Canada since assuming office two and a half years ago this week.
Last week at home in my riding of Bonavista-Trinity- Conception most of the constituents I met expressed to me their satisfaction with the way the economy has been managed. While they are of course unhappy that unemployment is not lower, as am I, the vast majority are pleased with the progress the Government is making. They know that better economic performance is the key to providing more help to the disadvantaged regions of the country. They know that the better economic performance since September, 1984, has allowed this Government to increase assistance to those in need.
Before reviewing the many actions this Government has taken to assist disadvantaged Canadians wherever they live, I would like to reflect for a minute on the dismal situation which existed before we assumed office. At that time the need for economic renewal was pressing. Some 15 straight years of budget deficits had swollen the national debt to $200 billion, a burden of almost $23,000 on every Canadian family. The national unemployment rate was almost 12 per cent and interest rates were far too high, discouraging both investment and consumer confidence. Finally, after almost 12 years of Liberal mismanagement the people of this country said they had had enough and overwhelmingly elected a responsible Government to administer their hard-earned tax dollars in a responsible manner.
In November, 1984, this Government set out its philosophy of responsible economic management in an agenda for economic renewal. Restoring fiscal responsibility was the starting point. We set out to get our fiscal House in order by reducing the deficit and slowing the growth of the national debt. This Government has restrained spending and managed its affairs more efficiently than our Liberal predecessors could have imagined, let alone accomplished. However, the Government's program for economic renewal has meant much more. We have introduced policies and programs which provide a better framework for growth and job creation, and which are less of an obstacle to change and innovation. They contribute as well to improving Canada's competitive position world-wide.
March 3, 1987

We have adopted policies which help small business and foster entrepreneurship and risk-taking. Yet for the new policies to succeed we knew they had to be fair and consistent with the basic sense of compassion, tolerance and justice which are characteristic of Canadians. That was the challenge and here are just some of the achievements.
Canada has enjoyed real economic growth averaging about 3.5 per cent during the last two and a half years. This is second only to Japan among the major industrial countries and it surpasses the growth of the U.S. Short-term interest rates are at their lowest level in nearly a decade and it is interesting to note that some articles appearing in the newspapers are saying this Government is on the right track.
Too bad that the Hon. Member who just spoke did not read some of those statements in today's paper. He would have seen that mortgage rates are down to their lowest level in the past 10 years. As a result, housing starts are up to an eight-year high. In my own Province of Newfoundland, the value of building permits in 1985 alone was 19.5 per cent higher. That represents an additional $30 million in construction activity. In the first 10 months of 1986, the value of building permits increased by another 13.5 per cent, representing an additional $18 million in construction activity. Nationally, inflation has been lowered to around the 4 per cent range. In Newfoundland, the inflation rate of 2.9 per cent is below even the national average. Nationally, the unemployment rate has dropped by two percentage points, and in Newfoundland it has fallen by 4.6 percentage points since this Government's election, from 23.8 per cent to 19.2 per cent. As I said at the beginning of my remarks, I am not very happy that the unemployment rate remains so high in my province but at least it has not increased by 9.9 percentage points as it did between February, 1980 and September, 1984, when the Liberals were last in office.
Finally, I would like to mention the important progress we have made in reducing the deficit. When this Government took office it inherited a deficit of $38.3 billion. Last year the deficit fell to $34.4 billion. This year we will further reduce the deficit to $32 billion. In our third year the deficit will be down to $29.3 billion. As some of my colleagues who spoke before me stated, this is the first time in 30 years that the deficit has declined for three consecutive years. I apologize to the members in the Opposition because I know that it pains them to hear this good news.
Clearly the Government's economic renewal program is working. It is delivering more growth, more jobs and more opportunity for Canadians now. The outlook for 1987 is proof of that. Canada's employment growth is expected again to beat all other major industrial countries. Canada should enjoy real output growth of 2.8 per cent, making this economic upturn the second longest of the post-war period. Inflation is projected to average less than 4 per cent.
The Budget-Mr. Johnson
Earlier I referred to the measures the Government has taken to assist disadvantaged Canadians. The Opposition would like the low income people of the country to believe that the Government does not care about their needs. Such individuals know that this is clearly not the case for they are benefiting from the Government's actions including the prepayment of the child tax credit of $454 per child. One million low-income people received this prepayment in November, 1986. Four million low-income families and individuals are now receiving the benefit of a refundable sales tax credit of up to $50 per adult and $25 per child. The child tax credit has been increased by 36.5 per cent or $140 per child, up from $384 in 1985 to $524 in 1987. The Government extended the spouses' allowance. Now 169,000 widows aged 60 to 64 who are in need receive this assistance. The Government extended the tax deduction for disability for 185,000 people.
These and other measures by the Government to assist low-income Canadians will be complemented and strengthened when our tax reform proposals are introduced in the spring. The Government is committed to increasing the number of low-income Canadians who do not pay personal income taxes. The Government is committed to making the tax system fairer and simpler for the benefit of average Canadians. In other words, more Canadians will pay less tax.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to comment specifically on the Government's economic record as it relates to my Province of Newfoundland. As I said at the outset, Newfoundlanders are pleased with the federal Government's performance in controlling federal spending, reducing interest rates, and continuing good financial management. The Government has already taken a number of steps to help address the concerns of my province. The historic Atlantic Accord treats Newfoundland as an equal partner in offshore development and creates the $300 million Canada-Newfoundland Development Fund. I am pleased that Bill C-6, an Act to implement the Canada-Newfoundland Atlantic Accord, passed third reading yesterday.
The Government has signed multimillion dollar economic and regional development agreements with Newfoundland, including $112.5 million for highways, $38.5 million for the pulp and paper industry, and $33.6 million for forestry resource development. For Atlantic Canada as a whole there is up to $1 billion in loan guarantees and low interest rates for certain investments in the region through the Atlantic Enterprise Program. Companies in Newfoundland are taking advantage of this program. On Friday I had the opportunity to announce benefits which two companies in my own riding will be receiving from this program.
In addition, $600 million in federal procurement provided to the region through the Atlantic Opportunities Program will also have a positive impact. For example, in my riding Terra Nova Shoes is, for the first time, now supplying footwear to the Department of National Defence. It is interesting to note

March 3, 1987
The Budget-Mr. Hovdebo
that the 9 per cent federal sales tax on fuel used by fishermen which had previously been removed has not been reinstated.
All these initiatives and others are part of a continuing effort by the Government to increase assistance to Atlantic Canada. One of my colleagues in the Opposition says that the sales tax on fuel has increased by 1 per cent. I remind him that that 1 cent is not applicable because fishermen and loggers, as well as the farmers of the country, will receive a rebate of that 1 per cent which is an excise tax. 1 was talking about sales tax.
It is true that we have come a long way in two and a half years, but it is true as well that we have a long way to go. This Budget shows that our agenda for economic renewal is working and will continue to work for the benefit of all Canadians.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to have the opportunity to speak immediately after a member of the Conservative Party who spent a good portion of his time suggesting that the new Budget will show lower income people how well off they are. In fact, the Fraser Institute, a very conservative-thinking institute, has suggested that the only two areas which managed to escape taxes are large corporations and the very rich. It looks as though the aim of this Budget is to increase taxes in the lower and middle-income areas without increasing taxes in the other areas. Higher income individuals and corporation taxes increased only very slightly. For instance, a couple with two children earning $15,000 paid only $407 in federal income taxes in 1985. In 1986-87 they will pay $770 in taxes. That is a 90 per cent increase. The taxes of those earning $20,000 was increased from $1,200 to $1,700, a 35 per cent increase. The federal income taxes of those earning $42,000 rose to $6,102, an increase of 32 per cent or $1,487. Those figures are an indication of how the Budget will affect lower income earners.
Let us look at higher income earners. The taxes of a couple earning $100,000 will only increase by $319 compared with the couple earning $15,000 whose taxes will increase from $407 to $770. The couple earning $100,000 will have only 2 per cent increase compared to the 90 per cent increase experienced by the couple earning $15,000. In fact, as a result of this Budget, taxes went down approximately 5 per cent for those earning $80,000, and decreased by 1 per cent for those earning $50,000. The Hon. Member who attempted to explain whose taxes were increasing has not read the Budget thoroughly to determine the levels of taxation. Those earning only $7,000, which is below the poverty level, face an increase of 148 per cent, which is the largest increase in the Budget. This Budget is not intended to help lower income Canadians but to help the very rich and the big corporations.
The Budget is not intended to eliminate the deficit but forms the centre piece in preparation for tax reform. While this Budget represents a monstrous tax grab of approximately $1 billion from people in the lower income areas of Canada, it is only the centre-piece on which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Government intend to implement tax reform in the next year or two.
Let us examine what has been happening with our tax system in the last two and a half years. The Government has increased taxes on lower income people through direct income tax as well as indirect taxes through increased excise sales tax on almost every item. In fact, the Minister of Finance proudly stands up to say that he will broaden the base of taxes on goods and services. Theoretically, the income tax base is as broad as it can be, but the Minister indicated that since it is unfair that 40 per cent of goods and services in this country are not taxed at all now, all goods and services will be taxed. Direct taxes on goods and services is regressive because those with low incomes will have to pay the same as those earning high incomes.
The tax structure in this country will impose very high taxes on the majority of middle class and lower income Canadians. The Government will introduce tax reform in which it will broaden the base by taxing goods and services while lowering income tax. Those who will be the most affected by tax reform that will increase in the tax on goods and services will be those who are living below the poverty line and earning less than $7,000 and do not pay any income tax.
Perhaps the Government hopes that just before the election Canadians will notice that their take-home pay is suddenly larger as a result of reduced income tax, but will not recognize that the total tax they have paid in the previous three years has risen by several hundred per cent.
The crisis in agriculture today has developed in the last number of years. However, it has been emphasized this year by the low commodity prices. There are two methods by which to increase the income of people who earn their living from resources which depend upon commodity prices. One is to increase the price of the commodity directly, and the other is to decrease the input cost of that item. The problem facing agriculture is that the sale of the commodity no longer covers the cost of production so that today even farmers who have no debts find themselves in a position where they can no longer make a profit.
While this situation was happening before the Government took office, in the last two and a half years that it has been in office it has not only been unable to increase the price of the commodity to help the situation, it has increased the input costs considerably. Today, inspections and government services which have been available to farmers for many years are no longer free. The Government has implemented a user-pay structure that is eroding the already small profits farmers have been making. The situation is such that there is now a story about the farmer who has won a million dollars in a lottery. When asked what he would do, he said that he would keep farming for a couple of years to get rid of the money. That is the situation facing farmers on the Prairies these days.
One of my neighbours told me that he has no debts but his net worth this spring will be $75,000 less than it was last year.
March 3, 1987

If this situation continues we will lose a whole generation of farmers. This Budget did not nothing to alleviate the problems farmers are facing. It did nothing to assist them to get over the hump. Therefore, more and more farmers can be expected to go under, either registering bankruptcy or being foreclosed in some way, or even walking off their farm and leaving what they have there. In fact, the Government, not necessarily in this Budget alone but over a period of time, has increased the burden the farmers must carry. For many farms to survive, the farmer or his wife must leave the farm to work in order to bring in some extra income to meet the costs of running the farm. This is becoming the norm for a larger and larger proportion of the farm population. In fact, more than 50 per cent of farms now have outside incomes which are the same as, or even more than, the farm income.
When this Government was elected back in 1984, it promised it would do something about those farmers who must get money from somewhere else in order to keep their farm operating. Section 31 of the Income Tax Act restricts the amount of outside income a farmer can use to keep his farm going. I know it is not right that a farmer should have to go and work at a job someone else could have, but in many cases that is the only way he can keep the farm going. The Government promised it would do something about Section 31 which allows the farmer to write off $1,000 against farm losses. A committee of this House unanimously recommended that that amount be raised to at least $10,000. The Government promised it would eliminate the limit entirely. Nothing was done. Therefore, farmers who are valiantly attempting to keep the farm going by working off the farm and using the money to pay their farm debts are being discriminated against by the Government.
Lately a number of farmers have had their income tax reviewed because at some time during the last 10 years they have purchased machinery and taken an investment tax credit at a level which the Government considers to be a little higher than they should have. If you had gone through one of these deals, Mr. Speaker, you would realize that what the farmers are doing is taking advantage of a tax law which is in place and which is legal. They turn in their old machinery, buy new machinery and receive a tax credit. They are now being blamed for making the best possible deal they could. It is not illegal. In fact, it is probably a very good Conservative philosophy. But these farmers are being questioned and many of them are being told they will have to repay some of the tax credits they have received over the years.
Tax reform seems to be the centre-piece of this Budget. The Government is increasing income tax and other taxes so that when the tax reform comes in, it will already be taking such a large portion of the incomes of middle and lower wage earners that they will be very happy to get some relief in that area.
There is nothing in the Estimates for the ice-breaker which was promised. There is nothing for the drug relief program
The Budget-Mr. Hovdebo
which was also promised. There is no money identified in these Estimates, or in the Budget, for child care. There is a lot of money provided for advice from people like Dalton Camp but there is no money for the main promises the Government has made over the years. There is nothing in the Budget to attack unemployment and nothing for regional disparities. There is nothing to help out those areas which have a large unemployment problem. This Budget is for the very rich and for the large corporations. The poorer among the population are feeling the results of the Government's philosophy, which is all in preparation for some fanciful tax reform, and if the plan works, as it has in the past, the burden of taxes on the lower wage earners will only increase.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for my colleague and friend from Prince Albert. I wonder if the calculations he gave from the Budget with respect to the percentages paid by the poor and so-called rich take into consideration the alternate minimum tax. As I gathered from his speech, they do not. I can tell from my riding that that alternative minimum tax is having quite a dramatic effect on the number of dollars people are paying in 1986. Can he tell me whether his figures reflect that?
Second, is the Hon. Member arguing in favour of, for example, a combine which would originally sell for $90,000 being sold for $140,000 just so the farmer could get the larger tax credit? Of course, that in effect means that the rest of us as taxpayers end up having to pay a lot more. Surely that is the same type of deal as the practice of some of these huge

March 3, 1987
The Budget-Mr. Thacker
companies which use the tax loopholes, which were originally an incentive, in an artificial way, which hurts the public's good.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, the figures I quoted on taxation were the figures which were presented in a brief by the Fraser Institute and also by the Federal Advisory Council on Welfare. Both groups are funded to some extent by Government. The brief shows the effect of federal income tax increases on those particular groups.
As far as the tax credit is concerned, many of the farmers who use those tax credits recognize them as wrong in some way. However, they were put there by the tax structure and, in most cases, the farmer accepted the deal which was given to him by the machine companies. I do not think it should have gone on. I am glad the Government is doing something about it. However, to go back 10 years and have these farmers repay these credits is creating a hardship which many of them will not be able to survive. It will force them into bankruptcy. What has happened in the farming community in the last few years is that many large farms have become over-extended to the extent that they have large debts which they are now unable to finance. If they are further burdened by the reclaiming of these large portions of tax, which are taxes not against them but which were within the law at that time, then they will be put into a situation which will not help the farming community as a whole in any way at all. I am suggesting not that we leave the tax credit but that we not go back and try to collect the tax from those farmers in the way that appears to be happening now.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad that we now have the New Democratic Party on record vis-a-vis action against farmers who took advantage of the tax credit for the purchase of machinery. This is a very serious situation in western Canada. The fact of the matter is that some machine dealers and some farmers knew exactly what they were doing. They artificially elevated the price of machinery. I know of some examples in which prices were elevated from $90,000 to $140,000. They knew that this was wrong. It is questionable as to whether the law should be ignored when it comes time to enforcing it. At any rate, I am glad to see the NDP onside with respect to that particular question.
I wish to offer my congratulations to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) on his third Budget. In terms of yearly Budgets he has clearly formalized the process. It has now been made easier for us by having the Estimates and the Budget at the same time. In this way we can more effectively question the Minister of Finance with respect to spending and how the money will be raised. It also makes the system much easier in terms of the response of provincial Governments. They now know what they will be receiving.
There are a number of reasons why I think this is a good Budget. There is no doubt that, in general, the economy has improved dramatically over the course of the tenure of the
Minister of Finance. One of the reasons for this is that Canadians exercise their sovereignty and change their Governments. The first Budget of the Minister came out with an economic plan to cover the next four or five years. It gave a degree of certainty to business, something for which members of the business community asked. In this way they can make their plans, something that the first Budget allowed them to do. The two subsequent Budgets have kept on that track.
Some 677,000 new jobs have been created by Canadians as a result of increased confidence. This is a significant contribution to Canada and its well-being. It means that more revenue will be derived from income tax. It also means that fewer people will be on welfare and collecting unemployment insurance benefits. Unemployment has gone from well over 10 per cent to 9.7 per cent this year. It should be at 9 per cent by the end of this year. That is very significant. Everyone should be thankful that it is occurring. TThese are results which do not always occur just because of a change in federal Government or because of the actions of Government. They happen as a result of people having confidence in their country.
There is no doubt that the problem of regional disparity is serious. Even though I come from the west, I am thankful that Ontario is doing well. I am thankful that jobs are being created in Ontario. The Province is manufacturing jobs, which means that we can export more material. This helps our current account. It helps pay revenue into our tax coffers and it means less unemployment. I ask Hon. Members to imagine where the country would be if Ontario were having the same set-backs that we are having in the west. These setbacks are not as a result of government action but as a result of international commodity prices. If Ontario were in the same condition as the west, then we would see some two million to three million people unemployed. As a result, our social programs would not be worth the paper on which they are written. I think the nation should rejoice that Ontario is doing well rather than being envious.
In the late 1970s I could not understand the antipathy toward the west when we were doing so well. Young people from other parts of the country were moving into Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and B.C. To my mind that was good for the country. We were hot at that time. We were able to pay more money to help the disadvantaged regions. The same is true today. I can say without hesitation that I am thankful that Ontario is doing well. It bodes well for the country.
Interest rates are at their lowest in 10 years. That is very significant. It is not something which has occurred simply by happenstance or by accident. It is a major historic event for Canada. I lived through the period of time when interest rates were around 21 per cent under the Liberal-NDP coalition. Those interest rates killed people. Indeed, they are still killing people literally and figuratively today because of bad economic policy.
It costs us less to service the national debt when interest rates are down. The individual businessman who almost always takes out loans from his bank now has more money in his
March 3, 1987

pocket because of lower interest rates. A family with a $50,000 mortgage now has $125 to $130 more in their pockets each month than they would have had if the Liberals and the NDP were in power. This gives families more disposable income. It gives them more freedom to decide how they will spend their money as opposed to a financial institution taking it away from them in terms of high interest rates or in terms of the Government of whatever political stripe deciding how to spend it for them.
I now wish to refer to a part of the Budget which has not received any coverage in the media which, in my judgment, is of historic significance. In terms of program expenditures and tax revenues the deficit is down by $1.3 billion. When we came to power, the deficit to service the national debt was huge, but program spending under the Liberals and the NDP reached the level of being several billion dollars more than tax revenue. Once we are into the next fiscal year we will see a surplus between our tax revenues and our program expenditures. Once we have balanced Budgets in terms of programs and revenues we can then truly work on the national debt and solve that problem because our economy is growing. The national debt will then make up a smaller and smaller percentage of the gross domestic product.
I would like to say a few words about the social dimensions of the Budget. I think one has to consider them as a package. There is no doubt that when we get to the end of the five years-and indeed we are at that level today-the people who are poor will have more cash in their pockets than if we had remained under the Liberal-NDP coalition. The tax credit and the refundable sales tax program in tandem, for example, mean that a single mother raising a child has something in the order of $44 more in her pocket as a result of the last Budget than she would have had under the status quo. That is a principle which I fully support.
I am prepared to argue with anyone at any public forum across the land with respect to this subject. The theory of the previous administration, and certainly the idea of the Liberals and the NDP, was that social programs should be available to everyone. Then, presumably because of a progressive tax system, the cost of them is taxed back from the rich. That has never been the case. The tax system never brought in 100 per cent of the funds needed to cover these programs. Therefore, whether we consider family allowances or old age security, we find the rich getting richer and richer because of the Liberal-NDP philosophy. Our philosophy is that those who are genuinely poor should get cash. Those of us who are earning beyond a certain threshold do not need to have family allowance or old age security, and, therefore, they ought not to be paid.
When there are limited dollars they should be applied where they are really needed. I must say that I stand embarrassed in the House when I hear Members of Parliament arguing for a
The Budget-Mr. Thacker
continuation of the family allowance to be paid to those of us who are Members and receive a basic allowance of $57,000.
I want to deal with the argument that the NDP raised that magically somebody else out there is much richer than those of us who are Members of Parliament. The facts do not show that. I wish to read into the record data from the summary of income tax returns prepared by Statistics Canada. A person who earns $15,000 in total income is in the 55.42 percentage group. That means that only about 45 per cent of the people earn more than $15,000. I am talking about the people who file tax returns. A person who earns $25,000 is at the 78 per cent level. That means that fewer than 22 per cent of taxpayers earn more than $25,000. Many people in the country earn approximately $35,000. A person who earns $35,000 is at the 91.62 percentage level. Fewer than 9 per cent of taxpayers earn more than $35,000. A person who earns $50,000, which is a little less than MPs, is at the 98.18 percentage group of tax filers. Fewer than 2 per cent earn over $50,000.
The fact of the matter is that there is no mythical rich person that the NDP harp about whose taxes we can increase and thus reduce the deficit or for whom we can provide new programs. It has to come from you and me, Mr. Speaker.
The Government and the Minister of Finance deserve universal support and credit for the fact that now people have clear in their minds the relationship between program expenditures and taxes. When a new program is offered, we also offer a tax to the people. 1 hope that that is fixed in their mind so that when the Liberals and the NDP offer all types of rich programs they will also say to people that the tax rates will have to go up, ladies and gentlemen. Which do you choose? If the question were put to the people in that manner, they would often say that the program is not needed. We would prefer to keep the money in our own pockets and decide how to spend it rather than give it to the Government to decide.
In terms of agriculture from a western perspective, 1 have to say that never has a Government allocated so much money to one sector, and particularly that sector being western Canada. Spending in agriculture is up by some 62 per cent from the previous administration. That does not include the $1 billion expenditure that is coming up. The sugar-beet producers in my riding would have been forced out of the industry had there not been government help. They received $10 million or $11 million allocated under the tripartite stabilization program, and it saved that industry. I hope that we can come up with an even better program once the Canadian Tariff Board brings in its recommendations or the options that will be available. Contrast that with what was done by the previous administration when the sugar-beet industry in Ontario went down the tube. The previous administration was not there to help that industry when it was needed. But the Conservative Government was there when that industry in Manitoba and Alberta needed help.

March 3, 1987
The Budget-Mr. Thacker
In terms of farm fuel, when my relatives fill their fuel tank it now costs them $40. Under the Liberal administration it cost them $115 to fill their tank.
I have to say with some regret that the population in western Canada does not genuinely appreciate the significance of the removal of those taxes on the oil industry. The reason is that they feel that the taxes were put on improperly and that we have righted a wrong. We are not receiving the political credit, but even without it the population in western Canada has to appreciate the fact that when the Government puts on taxes it is very seldom, if ever, that they are removed. I am not aware of one tax that has been removed, including the temporary income tax that was put on to finance the First World War. It has never been removed.
The natural gas and liquids tax, the incremental oil revenue tax, the Canadian ownership special charge, the crude oil export charge, the petroleum compensation charge were all charges on the oil industry that were put on by the previous administration as its policy which it claimed was the National Energy Program. Of course, it was not that. It was the western oil and gas taxation program, which benefited the rest of the country. A national energy program may well be necessary. But if it involves taxes, it should be a tax that applies across the country on a Btu basis so that the energy would be picked up whether it is solar or electrical energy from Ontario or Quebec, or western petroleum energy. That would be a true national energy program, and it may well be needed in the future.
Let us not forget, and I hope that westerners will not forget, that the six or seven taxes were removed. That is a significant event. The difference in revenues is that under the Liberals approximately $5 billion from these taxes were withdrawn, and now it is under the general program where we all pay a few taxes, particularly on profits, amounting to about $500 million. That is a substantial benefit. The money is left in western Canada and is applied by these companies and people as they decide rather than as Ottawa decides.
I have a short comment to make with respect to gasoline. No matter what province it is, the provincial Governments are now pulling far more taxes out of gasoline than the federal Government. Therefore, the people of Ontario and Quebec who pay a lot of money for their gas should be looking to their provincial Liberal Governments that have imposed high gasoline taxes. There is nothing to say that those Liberal Governments could reduce the provincial gas tax. It is not the resource that is being taxed. It is a way of raising money from the people. If the Governments truly wish the people to have cheaper energy, they should remove those taxes.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I feel a question coming on.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My colleague opposite should realize that there is no tax in terms of energy in the Alberta Government, at least to this point. Who knows what future Budgets may hold. Because of the hard times that are now hitting, I suspect that there will have to be some tax increases. But it is a free
choice by the provincial Governments whether or not to put a tax on gasoline. Rather than complaining about the federal Government and its role in taxing gasoline, they should be looking to reducing the provincial taxes.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I wish to direct a question to my hon. friend. He is right in assuming that many people in western Canada feel that the PGRT was a tax that should not have been imposed. By its removal, the Government was merely righting a wrong. I also listened to the list of taxes which the Hon. Member said had been removed. As I mentioned yesterday in Oral Question Period, that is old news. I do not think western Canadians are impressed by the actions of the Progressive Conservative Party in respect of the National Energy Program. They are very concerned about the energy situation in western Canada. They want to know whether the Progressive Conservative Government will honour its commitments. They want to know whether the Conservatives will honour their election promises or whether the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) will honour his commitments and do something. To date nothing has been done, and they feel betrayed.
What purpose is served in trying to portray western Canadians as being concerned or in a state of euphoria over a reduction or a removal of those particular taxes? Western Canadians are concerned about what the federal Government will do to help their energy sector.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no doubt in agreeing with my friend that we are not getting any political credit for having taken off those taxes. That is absolutely true, but frankly I think it is wrong.
Western Canadians should be thankful that they have been removed. Had they not changed Governments, those tax rates might have been juggled a bit but they would still be there. We have taken off those taxes. We have actually eliminated the statutes so that if a future Government of whatever stripe tried to put those taxes back on, it would have to submit fresh legislation. Of course in that event we from the West would fight it and let the bells ring, as we did when the last piece of legislation was brought in.
Within the fiscal restraints, which the Hon. Member realizes still involves a deficit of some $32 billion, and hopefully dropping to under $30 billion next year, there is a question about how much can be done. Is it the position of the Liberal Party that the Government should increase the deficit to give help to oil companies? Is it its view that we should put taxes on the entire Canadian population and then transfer money to the oil companies?
My own view is that for 50 years oil companies searched for and found oil. They produced it, sold it, paid higher than average salaries, and made a profit at $2.35 per barrel. That went on from the 1930s-1940s until recent times. Then in the late 1970s prices skyrocketed with OPEC prices up to $35 to
March 3, 1987

$36 per barrel. Now it is down to $20 to $24 Canadian per barrel.
The fact of the matter is that the input costs of everyone, including the oil companies, were too high in that big bubble. They put up large office towers. There were expensive contracts, subcontracts, and farming agreements. They paid too much for their land. They had to rachet down, and they have done it. From here on there is no reason that the oil companies cannot do quite well. When they start to do well, so does the service industry.
If my friend was talking about the service industry, I agree that they are the people at the front lines. When the Liberals were in power, we said that the program would not hurt large multinational companies. We said that it would ultimately hurt tiny Canadian producers. Our prediction was absolutely correct, to the enth. We told people that they would suffer because an artificial market was being created by the previous administration. Unfortunately our predictions have come true.
The adjustment process is almost over. We have a base from which we can build into new prosperity in the future.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a few comments to make with regard to Liberal hypocrisy. 1 listened to them talk about the price of gas. What unmitigated gall. I can recall the 1980 election, lying to the Canadian people that they were going to give them cheap gas. Between 1980 and 1981 gas went up 60 cents per gallon under the Liberal-NDP coalition.
The Grits and the Socialists were not the least bit interested in getting cheap gas for Canadians. They allowed it to go up 60 cents per gallon. Look at them now; they ridicule us because it goes up a few cents. Gas is a lot less today than it was when the Liberals were in power.
I congratulate the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker) who talked about agricultural problems. 1 have listened to much rubbish and nonsense today in the debate about the Conservative Party having written off the west, that nothing is going into the west. I could spend two hours this afternoon reading off what is going into the west-programs beyond belief. They have the gall to say that nothing is going into the West. I do not understand why the media do not do a job on the Liberal Party.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 rise on a point of order. If the Hon. Member made a motion to allow him to spend two hours reading the benefits bestowed by the present Government upon western Canada, I think Hon. Members on this side of the House would be agreeable.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Winnipeg- Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie) may continue with his question or comment.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps the Table Officers could assist in this motion. I would most certainly be agreeable to doing that. I might have been a little short on my time; perhaps I should have said three hours or four hours. If it
The Budget-Mr. Thacker
could be arranged, I would be only too glad to accommodate the Liberal Party.
The Liberals mentioned that we were doing nothing for western farmers or for agriculture. I should like to give one example. CIDA is to spend $450 million on Canadian food products, according to a recent announcement in Winnipeg. The projects funded by CIDA include $310 million to the World Food Program for the next two years; $89 million worth of canola oil and technical assistance to India over the next five years; $13 million worth of canola oil as food aid to Pakistan this year; and $40 million over the next three years to support the activities of the Winnipeg based Canadian Foodgrains Bank, in addition to $8 million already donated this year. The list goes on and on.
Turning to more aid for agriculture in the West, a program of $1 billion of assistance is being formulated to supplement the cash flows of grain farmers affected by the drop in world wheat prices. Through a series of rebates, all federal sales and excise taxes have been removed from farm fuels. Farmers now receive a full exemption of up to $500,000 from capital gains realized on the sale of farm property. This is to assist them with retirement, but the Liberal Party and the New Democratic Party are opposed to farmers having pensions. They have made that quite clear on numerous occasions.
Legislation has been passed to create farm debt review panels. The Government has made a record pay-out of $580 million under the Western Grain Stabilization Program. The Western Grain Stabilization Act has been amended to provide interim payments to farmers so that they can receive much needed cash in time for spring seeding. Grain farmers received $150 million in assistance for crop damage caused by drought and grasshoppers. Livestock producers received $48 million.
Interest rates are at their lowest level since 1979, saving farmers millions of dollars. We have doubled the maximum payments to farmers for storable crops under the Advance Payments for Crops Act. Farmers who have no choice but to leave the land will now be eligible for transition and training assistance under the new Rural Transition Program.
The Government has brought in commodity based mortgages and the shared risk mortgage program to assist western farmers. We have concluded new grain deals with the U.S.S.R., Brazil, and Egypt. The WGTA producers' freight rate has been maintained at the 1985-86 crop year level, saving farmers over $40 million. Action has been taken to reduce European beef imports into Canada by 55 per cent. A new long-term dairy policy has been announced. Sugar-beet producers will receive stabilization help as a result of a new federal-provincial-producer program.
I see that my time is up, Mr. Speaker. If it could be arranged for me to read this information into the record-and I will contact my office to get the rest of the material-I would say that three hours would cover about half of it.

March 3, 1987
The Budget-Mr. Boudria

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity this afternoon to participate in the debate on the Budget. After listening to speeches from some Tory Members across the way, particularly the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie), who disguised his questions to the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker) in such a manner that he was really delivering a speech instead of asking a question, one has to wonder whether the Member was talking about the same Budget that we are talking about. We are talking about the slimmest budgetary document ever introduced in this House in recent years. We are talking about a Budget that had very little in it, not only very little in terms of content but very little in terms of substance. 1 know that does not bother the Tories in this House. Not to have substance suits them just fine, as we all know. Is there anything so bad about having a Budget with nothing in it, some Tories have asked? Maybe there isn't, but then why bother presenting one? Why didn't the Minister just present a press release and a Ways and Means motion, I ask you, Mr. Speaker? Perhaps Tory Members who are wondering what is wrong with a Government without a vision would then know the answer. The mere fact that they ask suggests and tells me why the Government is in serious trouble.
Let us talk about the Government. Since it came to power in 1984, the public debt has risen from $175 billion to $300 billion. That is a $125 billion increase or a 40 per cent increase in three and a half years. Forty per cent of the debt of the country has been generated while the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has been in that position. Maybe Tory Members can make copies of my speech and give them to their constituents. Constituents have a right to know about this kind of activity. We should remember that the Government is talking to us about what it claims is lowering the deficit. I have some difficulty with the way Tories define lowering the deficit. First they take over and the deficit is supposed to be $34 billion. Immediately after that they say the deficit is supposed to be $38 billion, then they lower it to $36 billion and tell us they have saved some money. I have a hard time with that, and I am sure you do too, Mr. Speaker, being the non-partisan person that you are. The deficit was then lowered, according to the last Budget, to $29 billion. But the Government changed its mind and said no, it could not deliver on that. The deficit will be $32 billion. When the Tories could not meet that, they introduced the next Budget and said the deficit would be under $30 billion. We will have it at $29 billion some odd. Do you know how the Tories can achieve this, Mr. Speaker? They will do it in two ways. First, by selling off Crown corporations.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Good.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
A Member opposite said good. Selling off the furniture to pay the rent is Tory economics. Let the record show that the Tories across said good to selling off the furniture to pay the rent. Second, the Tories are accelerating
remittance procedures so that businesses and municipalities have to remit twice a month. I am sure the Hon. Member for Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid) is concerned about this. I will repeat it slowly so that he will understand. Municipalities will now have to remit twice a month. This will cause major disruptions to municipalities and to large businesses. It will create one extra payment at the end of the year, which is the only reason that the Government will be able to get the deficit below the infamous $30 billion, something it has been striving for.
Let us talk about gas taxes. In the great constituency of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell, having an automobile is not a luxury. I represent a rural riding, Mr. Speaker.

In a riding such as mine, which is about 100 kilometers long from east to west, a car is no luxury. As you know, Mr. Speaker, because you do have the opportunity to drive through my riding when coming to Ottawa-and by the way I would encourage you to make frequent stops in my riding and spend all the money you like. This is good for the local economy. However, for my constituents, owning a car in order to move around, to go to work, as some of my constituents who are present today and are following this debate would know, having a car is important for earning their livelihood. Indeed it is important for my electors because they cannot use any public transit system.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why not?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) asks why. I know she knows the answer, but I will give the answer because the Tories probably do not understand and I am glad she asked me to explain. Obviously the Minister of Finance thinks the whole country is served by the TTC. He is wrong. There is no Toronto Transit Commission in the riding of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell. If you want to travel from one end of the riding to the other, you have to use your car. If you go to work, you have to use your car. Those people have the same right to live as does anybody else even though they do not have the TTC the way the Minister of Finance thinks we all do.
What has happened since the Conservatives have taken over? Since the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) have taken over, gas taxes have increased by 4.5 cents a litre. I say to the Hon. Member for Brampton- Georgetown very slowly again, that is 18 cents per gallon.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And how much tax came off?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Eighteen cents a gallon may remind him of something. A preceding Tory Government was turfed out of office because of an 18 cents a gallon gas tax, and the same thing will happen to this Government.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
How much tax has been taken off?
March 3, 1987

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Let me talk to you about the regions of the country. Again the riding of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell has been well served by the Canadian Industrial Renewal Board.

The CIRB program, Mr. Speaker, was beneficial to my constituency; we were given grants to modernize our textile industry, our footwear industry, so it could better compete with foreign industries. What happened? As soon as this Conservative Government came to power, against all those promises they made during the election, bang!, Mr. Speaker, the grants were cancelled. The CIRB program was abolished by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). And I am certain Hon. Members from Quebec, Hon. Members from eastern Ontario and from areas where there is a textile industry know there was a lot of work to be done. I, for one, and my constituents were hoping that in their last Budget he would have something to say, that the Minister of Finance would say that yes, it was worthwhile trying to save the footwear industry, that yes, the textile industry should be maintained. It was not to be so. Instead, we had a very hollow document, as hollow as Tory policy.
I would now like to say a few words about poverty, Mr. Speaker. There are now four million Canadians living below the poverty line. There is no reference to those Canadians in the budget I have here. Not a single word. And this is unacceptable.

The Budget-Mr. Boudria

Mr. Speaker, I would like to describe briefly those who will have to carry the tax burden. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after the remarks of the Hon. Member we have to get a number of facts and figures straightened out. Canadian people are entitled to an honest explanation of who is responsible for starting the uncontrolled spending and who is the king of deficits. The Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition, the Member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Turner), took over as Minister of Finance in 1972. At that time there was a surplus of $700 million in our current account. When he left in 1975 there was a deficit of almost $5 billion. The trend continued and we inherited a $38 billion deficit generated by the kings and queens of deficit, the Liberal Party.
If we had left everything that we inherited in place, if we had changed absolutely nothing, the debt for 1986 would have been $42 billion. We have reduced the debt by $10 billion, which is an excellent start. If the Liberal Party had been allowed to continue its policies, this country would have been turned into another Argentina or Mexico. That is the route we were taking.
The Hon. Member across the way mentioned something about Crown corporations selling furniture. I would like to give some statistics on the success story of de Havilland. Over the last decade the taxpayers of Canada watched $830 million of direct federal assistance poured into de Havilland to help keep it alive. Today, under the management of Boeing, sales and employment have increased. The Liberal and New Democratic Parties have said that if we sold de Havilland to Boeing it would collapse and everyone would lose their jobs. This has not happened. It has been the success story of the year. They have recent contracts which will increase employment by 250 jobs throughout Canada, 100 of which will be in Winnipeg. That should infuse about $11 million into the Canadian economy.
We know all about the Liberal Party's philosophy on Crown corporations. They did not even know how many Crown corporations they had when they were in power. They could not tell us the number of Crown corporations. After about six months of hammering away we finally got a count and found out that there were over 400 Crown corporations. What on earth did we need 400 Crown corporations for? The Liberal
March 3, 1987

bureaucracy could set up a Crown corporation on its own. It had a free hand to do anything it wanted to. We are going to get rid of a lot more unnecessary Crown corporations. We are going to sell excess land and buildings. We are making an honest and concentrated effort to reduce the deficit, which would have reached $42 billion this year.
Those are a few facts which should be on the table with regard to who created this huge deficit. We did not create it. We inherited it and are dealing with it. Every federal Government Department is reducing expenditures and cutting out waste and mismanagement. For the first time in the history of the Auditor General's report he has commended us for making an honest and concentrated effort for eliminating waste and mismanagement within the Government. We will receive more glowing reports from the Auditor General.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that was pretty hard to take. We heard a Tory saying that selling off Crown corporations is always the right thing after they sold Teleglobe for something like six times the earnings. Those people who pretend to be the friends of business and to know what they are doing in the business world sold a Crown corporation for five or six times its earnings. That is really a bit much to take. It is also difficult to listen to Tories pretending to be such able managers. They forget to tell us that the only two banks to have collapsed in the last half a century collapsed under the administration across the way with two Ministers of Finance looking on. They have no lessons to teach on this.
The Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine referred to the deficit king and talked about waste and mismanagement. I want to talk a little bit about waste and mismanagement too. I was not going to, but I have been provoked so I will have to. The Government instituted the $500,000 capital gains exemption, which will cost $800 million and will benefit the rich. It bailed out two banks at a cost of $1.6 billion. It gave $200 million to the Hongkong Bank of Canada and spent $41 million to create a monument in Port-Cartier which is euphemistically called the Port-Cartier prison. It spent $2.3 million on the so-called Stevens inquiry, $1 billion for the Gulf-Reichmann deal, and $2.7 million for new uniforms for the Armed Forces. Those are the uniforms that smell. Remember those, Mr. Speaker?
The Government is spending $10 million a year for three years for Mr. Reisman and free trade, which will probably lead us exactly nowhere. It spent $12 million on advertising to convince us that surrendering our sovereignty to the Americans is in our best interests. That is Tory politics. The Government has put $15.1 million in the Budget for cabinet Ministers' staff which has doubled since the Government has been in office. It spent $2.6 million on the Shamrock Summit so we could hear the Prime Minister and Ronald Reagan singing to us on TV. My television has not worked the same since. The expense for an office for the Prime Minister's wife is $100,000 a year.
The Budget-Mr. Boudria
We are paying $250,000 a year for the salary of Dalton Camp who was hired in September of 1986 to straighten the Government out, and it has been in a nosedive ever since. I want my money back for that Dalton Camp nonsense and so do the taxpayers of my riding. If there is a king of mismanagement, deficit and improper financing, it has to be the Conservative Government across the way.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria). I heard him speak of government waste, and I think it is important that we make clear to the Canadian people the extremely difficult circumstances we found ourselves in when we came to office a brief two years ago. We were faced with interest payments on the debt we inherited and payments for a social net which absorbed 83 per cent of all our revenue. We were left with roughly 17 per cent of discretionary spending cuts with which to pare our deficit down.
To the credit of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), he has done a remarkable job in little over two years. He has pared the annual deficit down by 24 per cent and is continuing to do an excellent job on that. We are seeing the results of that sound fiscal management reflected in the market-place. We are seeing increased investor confidence and the creation of 25,000 jobs per month since we were elected. It is important to remember that of the 25,000 jobs, 70 per cent are long-term. The record of the previous Government was the creation of 7,500 jobs a month in its last term, 83 per cent of which were short-term, or 24-week wonders, to allow people to earn unemployment benefits and leave them frustrated.
I urge the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) to consider the impressive record of the Government. Mortgage rates are down to below 10 per cent for the first time in 17 years. Interest rates are down 4 per cent. We have the fastest growing economy of all OECD countries, including Japan, and the fastest job-creation of all OECD countries, including Japan. While much has to be done, it is like a breath of fresh air when we reflect on the record of this Government in such a brief period, considering the morass we inherited.

Perhaps the Tories basically want to cut off many of those programs that we established. As a matter of fact, the House will recall that they tried to deindex senior citizens' pensions. I will not repeat what Solange Denis said on the steps of Parliament Hill because you would not allow me, Mr. Speaker. But most Canadians know well the true Tory agenda.
Let me deal with the so-called job-creation of the Tories since they have been in power. We are told that 115,000 new jobs have been created. We also know that 127,000 new jobs

March 3, 1987
The Budget-Mr. Harvey
were created in Ontario, primarily in the southwestern part of that province. This means there is a deficit of 12,000 jobs for the rest of the country, including the area I represent. Mr. Speaker, I am sorry that the Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie) has departed. He talked about these great deficits and how the Conservatives brought them under control. The Conservatives do not have a monopoly on deficit control in this country.
The Hon. Member has returned and perhaps he is interested in knowing that in Saskatchewan, between 1944 and 1964, the CCF Government of Tommy Douglas and Woodrow Lloyd had a balanced budget and often had a surplus. That continued between 1964 and 1971 under Ross Thatcher, a Liberal Premier. During Allan Blakeney's term as Premier of that province between 1971 and 1982, there never was a deficit. I say to my hon. friend from Winnipeg that in Saskatchewan, in terms of deficits, Tory times are tough times. In terms of deficits, Tory times are tough times as they were in the 1930s under R. B. Bennett. If he wants to see patronage, if he wants to see wild spending, and if he wants to see incompetence, he can come to Saskatchewan and talk to Grant Devine.
