subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank you for giving me the opportunity to address this House and all my fellow Canadians to comment on the budget brought down by our Government. This budget easily proves in my opinion that Canada has become the best country in the world in the space of only two and a half years.
We promised two and a half years ago that a Conservative Government would take Canada from one of the last among industrialized countries to the head of the pack.
I think that we can be proud of the fact that, after two and a half years, whatever the Liberals might say, the closest competitor of Canada as far as economic performance is concerned is Japan. This is no dishonour for a newcomer among countries with positive economic indicators since Japan has an outstanding performance.
Mr. Speaker, before speaking directly about the budget itself and our continuing objective to make Canada the best country in the world and to maintain it at its present level, I would like to try to show, based on the record of the Liberal Party and its stated intentions for the future, that it is absolutely impossible to have any confidence in the comments made by the Official Opposition about this budget.
Afterwards, I shall try to outline, not the record of the New Democratic Party, but its true intentions, show the way it contradicts itself on many issues and prove that these people cannot have our trust or our support.
When we look at the record of the Liberal Party, we find that, after 12 or 15 years under a Liberal Government during the last two decades, the debt had increased to $23,000 per family. This means interests of $70 million a day which Canadians must pay, or $3 million in interests an hour because of the wasteful spending of the Liberals.
Right now, the Grits, the Official Opposition have all the answers. The Liberal Opposition have among other things the solutions to the serious economic problems this Government is now overcoming.
It is important, if we are to analyse the credibility of their statements, Mr. Speaker, to check on what the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) stated in 1974-75. He had this to say: "We must do everything-he was then Minister of Finance-we must do everything possible to stop the increase in Government expenditures. As in the past, we will endeavour to reduce wages, limit Public Service growth, and approve only the most important of new programs."
So far so good. But what 1 find interesting, Mr. Speaker, is that the year after that statement was made, the federal deficit had increased 150 per cent. In other words, such a performance was no great shakes.
One only has to read the pre-budget statements of the Leader of the Official Opposition-and I will spare you, Mr. Speaker, the statements made by former Liberal Prime Ministers-to quote once more from the Leader of the Official Opposition, some 10 years later. His speech has not changed.
There is program duplication, while other programs are not viable. Some Government activities are wasteful. All this, Mr. Speaker, from the Official Opposition. We have programs which no longer serve any purpose, which are no longer useful, and I will put the axe to them. That was in 1984.
March 3, 1987

I was listening a few minutes ago to my Liberal colleague who had doubts as to whether we had changed their programs.
I could spend two hours speaking about program changes this Government has made. We could speak about the Canadian Jobs Strategy, that great program that is based first and foremost on the private sector. Instead of providing subsidies which remain fruitless and never create jobs, most of our programs are aimed at small- and medium-sized businesses whose main purpose is to create permanent jobs.
All this to say that when the Official Opposition formed the Government they showed arrogance and contempt towards everyone, including Parliamentarians and members of provincial and municipal governments. My honourable friend mentioned his political contribution to levels other than federal and I could tell him a thing or two myself about it. I might have an opportunity to do so later on.
Mr. Speaker, 1 find unfortunate that the opposition should refer to opinion polls at every opportunity. As a matter of fact, we are likely to have about 20 more of them before the next election. Personally, I trust the Canadian people, when the time comes, to know how to differentiate between demagogy and achievements and between lying and telling the truth.
I will not deprive myself of the pleasure of quoting Mr. Gilles Baril who served his fellow citizens with distinction at the provincial level and who has made an analysis which I feel fully deserves to be conveyed to all my fellow Quebecers.
"Federal Liberals, these clever masters of institutionalized patronage, for 20 years put their friends in charge of various federal departments. From the ordinary village Post Office through the CBC, the Crown corporations, the RCMP, the Civil Service and the great Deputy Minister, they all belonged and still belong to the Liberal family. Canadians have quickly forgotten the red cliques, their gimmicks, their faked projects such as the Canada Works-"
-which, by the way, no longer exists, Mr. Speaker. The Canada Works Program was abolished by our Government, Mr. Speaker.
"-in which the uncle, the aunt, the cousin or the organizer of the Liberal candidate campaign was involved."
-Make work programs which never amounted to anything and never created permanent jobs.
"Canadians, according to Mr. Baril, have quickly forgotten the "Louix IX" style of the former Prime Minister, his trips and parties, the fact that his country was ruined by high interest rates, high inflation and high unemployment. They have also forgotten that Liberals have been the champions of public fund waste and dilapidation, causing Canada to fall from the third to the seventeenth rank among industrialized nations."
Mr. Speaker, we brought it up from the seventeenth to the second place. This is quite a record in two and a half years; we could have made that promise two and a half years ago, but we would have been accused of being over optimistic, but indeed the facts are there. International organizations maintain that at present Canada is the best country in the world after due consideration of all economic parameters. This is obviously
The Budget-Mr. Harvey
exasperating for the Grits. I am telling them not to be that nervous because we will not harm them. We will continue to take action on basic issues.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, we must carry on with our policies in spite of the fact that demagogy-and I think that it will be short-lived-is now more popular than the achievements of this Government. We must not despair because there is an increasing number of responsible individuals.
I have here an editorial from Le Devoir blaming the Liberal Party, especially their Leader, for not having been bold enough in their decisions on certain economic issues. 1 will come to it in a few minutes, Mr. Speaker. They lack boldness because they want to play politics. Here are some examples. Can you, Mr. Speaker, define the position of the Liberal Party on free trade? Can you show me a statement indicating a consensus in the Liberal Party between the Hon. Member for Winnipeg- Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) who is the spokesman for his Party and the Hon. Member for Saint-Henri-Westmount (Mr. Johnston) who has been removed as the Liberal spokesman on trade issues because he agrees with the Government? He said that there was no choice, that we had to negotiate. It is to ensure a better future for Canada. Could you show me one single document, Mr. Speaker, where the leader of the Liberal Party has stated in any constructive way the position of his party on free trade? Absolutely not, Mr. Speaker. And 1 dare the Liberals to come up with any coherent document on which they all agree concerning our free trade policy, which is now endorsed by all the organizations in this country which care for the future prosperity of Canada. With regard to this issue, Mr. Speaker, we must not underestimate the importance of Canada as an economic partner for the United States. You can be sure that the United States are able to grasp the importance of this trade agreement as a model for multilateral negotiations which are a part of GATT. Here again, the Liberals have no policy.
On the Constitution, Mr. Speaker, how can you expect Quebecers to trust the proposals of the Liberal Party after having been put in their place and scorned by the previous Government? To think that the Liberals, at a recent convention, took position on the Constitution. One can hardly refrain from smiling at such news, but it is also somewhat sad. It is somewhat sad to hear the Liberals expound their views on the Constitution after having given us the brush-off for 15 years and having left us out in the cold in 1982.
Some say our Government has not conceived constructive policies for young people. I remember that in the spring of 1985, the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart), the defender of the disadvantaged, attacked us as a Government saying we did not have any program for students, for the young. Yet, youth unemployment has dropped several percentage points. Why? Because we have put forward the best programs, not one but seven programs with Challenge '86, Challenge '87 and Challenge '88 where we got unexpected and unbelievable success. Those programs are significant. They are very successful. Why? Because we appealed to the true

March 3, 1987
The Budget-Mr. Harvey
partners the Government can trust, those in the private sector. Our money, our programs are helping businesses, small and even big ones to create challenging jobs for young Canadians, jobs that are also relevant, and it is important to save our young people from being told when they graduate that they lack experience equivalent to their degree of training. But it is true, we have not heard anybody say anything about our programs for youth. In that area as in others, our performance has probably been exceptional.
For a laugh, Mr. Speaker, to help you understand and see the unbelievable void of the Liberal Party in all areas, you should read once more its resolution on the need for Canada to withdraw from the Atlantic Alliance. The Liberals who wasted so much public money, are telling us, in their resolution, that we should get out of the Atlantic Alliance in order to save money, when we know full well that neutral states spend much more on defence than members of the Alliance. This only means, as it was pointed out by the editorialist in Le Devoir, that the Grits programme is pure political opportunism. There is nothing the Grits will not do to get elected. But what is important to us is that the Government stays on the right track.
There is another major issue for Quebec, that is Bill C-22 on drug patents. Let us look at the position taken by these defenders of the needy, in particular that of the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie. You know that the pharmaceutical industry is located mostly in Quebec. This is not a drawback, we are here to defend Quebec interests and, consequently, the interests of the whole country. What is the position of the Grits on that Bill about pharmaceuticals? They do have a position. However, judging by what they said ... the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellette) said, in 1983, on Bill C-22: "that a series of amendments is actually under consideration, but the industry will have to accept some form of price control in order to protect the consumer".
That is what this Government has done. You should check the position of the Liberals on Bill C-22, concerning drug patents which give minimum security to companies that discover new products in Quebec. This will generate SI00 million in investments. Again, this is a blatant contradiction and I ask them to officially state their position. Ours as a government is clear.
Mr. Speaker-much has been said about tax reform. In case the Grits, the Official Opposition, do not know, the tax reform is already under way. It began with Bill C-23 which was passed before the Christmas recess. I do not make any unwarranted statements. I asked my colleagues to check which way the Official Opposition voted. Bill C-22 which was passed before the Christmas holiday provides for a minimum tax for the rich.
I therefore feel that in their new role as champions of the have-nots, Liberal Members could at least have congratulated the Government for that stance. They have voted against the collection of a tax on millionaires, on wealthy people.
I shall deal with the New Democratic Party in a few minutes, Mr. Speaker. There again, things are rather comical.
What I wish to say, Mr. Speaker, is that I could easily illustrate the record of the Liberals as regards their regional development policy. My region in particular has suffered deeply from never-ending federal-provincial disputes. There are some issues, Mr. Speaker, on which two, three, four or five electoral campaigns were run in my region and that we settled within two years. I have no lesson to take on regional economic development. People will tell me that our Government is neglecting regional economic development even if the estimates provided under that item in the budget have been increased by 4 per cent and even if the example which I will give shows quite well our concern for remote areas. I ask you to listen carefully.
Do you know that the last agreement signed by the Liberal Government provided for $1.4 billion spread out over 10 years? We have signed one providing for $1.6 billion over a five year period. And we are told that Quebec is losing $77 million one day and $97 million the next day. We are told that Quebec is also unfairly treated under our regional development policies.
All I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, is that I am sure slander and lying will only last so long.
Unfortunately, you are signalling that I have only two minutes left. It is really not enough.
With respect to the policies of the New Democratic Party, Mr. Speaker, we should ask them to tell us today why they want to keep the Auto Pact when a few months or a few years ago they advocated its review every five years? This is what I would like to know.
I am also eager to know the position of the New Democratic Party on the constitutional issue in Quebec, its exclusive rights on language matters. We will follow that very closely.
I would also like to know the official position of the New Democratic Party on Bill C-23 on a minimum tax and a sales tax credit to the underprivileged as well as on Bill C-22.
All this to say, Mr. Speaker, that this Government must maintain its thrust, maintain its direction, even though temporarily, it hurts of course to have the polls against us. do not want them to be nervous. I will not hurt them. But it is a good thing that they should hear the truth, because what is being peddled around is a bunch of lies, Mr. Speaker. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I wish to say a few words on behalf of all of us here in the Opposition who are present-at times one feels like a tiny minority.
The budget debate gives the House a unique opportunity to talk about the general direction in which we think the country should go. It is a little like the Throne Speech debate which also gives us that flexibility. It gives us a chance to speak on behalf of our particular constituency or region, because we all come from different realities. I come from a part of the country that is suffering economically. My constituents ask the question, "Where is Canada going as a nation?" During the parliamentary break last week I had a chance to have public meetings in my riding, in the village of Stenen, the towns of Norquay, Buchanan, Springside, and Mikado. All are very small communities.
The question that most people are asking is, "Where are we going as a country?" This is a country with tremendous wealth and potential, yet in the last 20 years our living standard has dropped from number one or two in the world to down to about tenth, eleventh, twelfth, or fifteenth position depending on how it is measured. They ask the question, "Where are we going as a nation? I think that we have a choice. We can either be a leader, or a follower; for much of our history, we have followed the American economy wherever it goes, or we can just get out of the way. Recently we have been getting out of the way as we
March 3, 1987

are pushed on shakes and shingles, on the U.S. Farm Bill, on softwood lumber, and starting yesterday on the question of potash. I do not believe it has to be that way. I believe that we can have a dream of a better tomorrow for ourselves, our children, and our grandchildren. I believe we can be a leader in the world. 1 believe that we can be a model for the rest of the world to follow. I believe that we have the potential, the intelligence, and the human spirit in this nation that if we had leadership, we could lead the world and be a model in the world of tomorrow.
I am concerned that the Budget does not provide that type of leadership. It has been described by everybody as a stand pat Budget, a safe Budget, a Budget that continues in the same direction. I am afraid that with that type of Budget we will not lead the world. I believe that we can modernize our economy. More money can be spent on research and development. We can specialize in certain areas. We can support our basic industries like farming, fishing, forestry, and resources. We can become a world leader if we have the dream and the vision.
As well, we lack a national spirit which unites us. All too often we are fighting, region against region, group against group, sector against sector. I do not see any evidence in the Budget brought down a couple of weeks ago that this will change.
As a matter of fact, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) have said time and time again that the economy is healthier now, that jobs are being created now, and that there is a great spin-off creating wealth from one part of the country to the other. That is just not the case. In most parts of the country there are more people unemployed and in desperate straits now than there were seven years ago, back in 1981.
I should like to refer to an article which appeared in The Globe and Mail on February 28. It indicated, for example, that in the last year-and I think Canadians would be interested in this information-more than 95 per cent of the additional jobs in Canada were located in the Province of Ontario. I may add that even Ontario development has not been very balanced, because 15 per cent of the people in northern Ontario are unemployed. Therefore, 95 per cent of the jobs created last year were created in southern Ontario, primarily because of the stimulation provided by the automobile industry which is going very well.
Between January 1986 and January 1987, the total number of jobs in the country rose by 137,000 according to Statistics Canada, but only 5,000 of those jobs were located outside the Province of Ontario. Another way of looking at it would be that 40 per cent of the people working today are working in Ontario and Ontario has only 36 per cent of the population of the country.
The Budget-Mr. Nystrom
If we look at the net number of people who are working, there are 2,000 fewer jobs outside Ontario today than there were a year ago on a seasonally adjusted basis, according to Statistics Canada. Therefore, 2,000 fewer people are working in nine provinces today than was the case a year ago, according to Statistics Canada.
When people in my part of Canada hear the Prime Minister or the Minister of Finance saying that there has been a creation of jobs, that there is new wealth, that there is a golden opportunity in the land, and that things are going well, they become very angry because it is not happening in Saskatchewan. It is not happening in western Canada, in Quebec, in the Atlantic provinces, or in northern Ontario. There is tremendous inequality in development in the country today. I do not see any evidence in the Budget to correct that tremendous imbalance. If it is not done soon, we will have growing regional inequities and regional alienation.
Last Friday a poll was published in The Globe and Mail which indicated that support in Manitoba for the separatist Confederation of the Regions Party had grown from 3 per cent to 7 per cent since October. Manitobans are feeling more and more alienated from not just the Government of Canada but from the national institution of Parliament and other Canadian institutions. This is a very serious issue.

I just heard the Hon. Member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Harvey) suggest in this House that everything is going fine now in the Canadian administration, thanks to this Tory Government. However, Mr. Speaker, would you take a very close look at the unemployment rate figures in Canada? A parallel can be drawn between the years 1981 and 1986. Everywhere in Canada unemployment rates are now higher than six years ago. And in provinces like Newfoundland, where six years ago there was a 13.9 per cent unemployment rate, the current rate is 20 per cent, a 6 per cent increase. And in Prince Edward Island, it went from 11.3 to 13.6 per cent. And in Saskatchewan, six years ago, there was 4.7 per cent unemployment and now the rate is 7.7 per cent. In my riding and in that of the Hon. Member for Assiniboine, the unemployment rate has almost doubled over the past six years.
A still more extreme example, Mr. Speaker, British Columbia had a 6.7 per cent unemployment rate six years ago, but now the rate is 12.6 per cent. And things are still worse in Alberta, where six years ago the unemployment rate was 3.8 per cent, as against 9.8 per cent now, Mr. Speaker. It is easy to see that we need a new regional development policy for Canada, because the only region in this country where everything is going right is southern Ontario. I have nothing against Ontario and Toronto men and women. I do not live in Toronto. There are other regions in Canada where the unemployment rate is much too high now.

Another concern is the sectoral problems. Canadian farmers are in great difficulty nowadays. Resource industries are in

March 3, 1987
Adjournment Debate
great difficulty. One needs only to talk to my Conservative colleagues from Alberta about the oil industry to understand the tremendous problems of that industry because of the fall in the price of oil around the world. We have the same problem in potash. To make things even more complicated, the American Department of Commerce decided yesterday to begin investigation of the anti-dumping petition in the United States. Just this morning the American International Trade Commission held hearings about whether or not there was injury to two New Mexican potash mines because of supposed subsidies in Canada, primarily by the Government of Saskatchewan.
Our resources are under attack by growing protectionism in the United States, yet we have a Budget which does not try to redistribute opportunity and money in any serious way to the regions of Canada which most need it.
I think they are making a big mistake and running the serious risk of not only the Government itself being defeated but of deepening regional alienation and division within Canada. I am very concerned about the possibility of a rise in western Canada of a western separatist Party which feels alienated from our system because western Canadians are not getting their fair share.

The same thing goes for Quebec. Five years ago, a referendum was held on Quebec's independence. For quite a while in that province, there was a movement towards independence, and now we have a Government with 57 Quebec members which, according to the most recent polls, has the support of only 14 per cent of Quebecers. There is certainly a major alienation from the federal Government in Quebec.
| English]
Then we have Newfoundland where the cod issue, in terms of the sell-out to France, has made Newfoundlanders so angry that they called open line shows questioning whether or not they should have joined Confederation in the first place and talking about the future of their province within the country. The issue has so angered Newfoundlanders that a Conservative Premier-and we all know how important is Party solidarity in Canada-is leading a crusade and a virtual war on his federal colleagues in Ottawa and against the great codfather, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie).
These things do great harm to Canada. I am afraid about the future of the country. As I said in the beginning, 1 think we have tremendous potential in Canada. If we had a vision, we could lead the world in terms of economic development. We could be a world leader in transportation, in the resource industries, in agriculture, in fisheries, and in forestry. However, we are not doing that. It is not Canada which comes up with new and innovative ideas, machines, and high technology. Instead, we import most of those things from Japan, the United States, and western Europe.

Forty years ago, during the Second World War, Germany, France and Japan were practically destroyed, but today, their economies are stronger than our own.
Mr. Speaker, it is six o'clock, so I will continue either tomorrow or whenever we resume debate on the budget.

subtopic: REFUGEES-CHANGES IN GOVERNMENT REGULATIONS. (B) REFUGEE DETERMINATION SYSTEM
REFUGEES-CHANGES IN GOVERNMENT REGULATIONS. (B) REFUGEE DETERMINATION SYSTEM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take up questions that I had the occasion of asking the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) yesterday in the House of Commons and followed up today with the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard). They dealt with the whole question of Canada's refugee policy. Essentially Canadians are getting confusing signals from the Government. On the one hand we have a system that is outdated with the present phenomenon facing Canada and facing the plight of refugees.
A special administrative review was put in place last May 21 by the former Minister of Immigration. Then the Government tinkered with the present parameters of that policy and announced changes some two weeks ago. It is promising legislation to set aside the system, creating a new independent refugee determination system. Today in media reports we learn of the Government's plan, already approved by the Planning and Priorities Committee, to usher in a second administrative review, or what The Globe and Mail and other newspapers refer to as general amnesty.
Canadians and refugees who are seeking asylum in Canada wish to know what kind of system we have. Over the last two years we have been trying to advocate bringing in a new, separate independent system apart from immigration, recognizing that an individual applying for landed immigrant status is pushed by certain criteria and that refugees seeking asylum are pushed by completely different motives and circumstances. That debate started with the Standing Committee on Immigration which submitted an umbrella report.
Rabbi Gunther Plaut provided a landmark report. Churches, organizations and immigrant aid societies across the country have given their input. The evidence is in. It clearly points toward the new system, yet we still have a Government that prefers to procrastinate. It is one that tinkered with the system a certain mode two weeks ago and then, as evidenced by this
March 3, 1987

amnesty or special administrative review, is tinkering with it in another way.
We are sending out two sets of signals. We have a front door policy and a back door policy. As I explained earlier, the policy is beginning to resemble a train with two sets of cabooses and which is going nowhere because each caboose is pulling in separate directions and each is playing one against the other. When we have a disorderly system and an inconsistent policy there is chaos. Chaos does two things. First, it allows greater abuse and allows those individuals who are making fraudulent claims to get away with them. Second, and more important, legitimate refugees are suffering as a result of the chaos, disorder and delay. We have individuals and families who have been waiting two, three and sometimes four years to get their lives determined. We need a system that is expeditious and fair.
The Prime Minister said on August 19 of last year when he was referring to the plight of refugees that "if we err, we will always err on the side of justice and on the side of compassion." Yet, as a result of changes made last week on which the Government hangs its hat, it is against fraudulent claims and false refugees. The entire country is, Mr. Speaker. Every Member of Parliament is against abuse in the refugee system or any other portion of our federal domain. We are not suggesting that we are in favour of fraudulent refugees, we are suggesting that there is a way of dealing effectively with the fraudulent refugee. Second, we are saying that we should not do the first to the detriment of legitimate refugees trying to normalize their lives and the lives of their families.
Because of the changes, rather than leaving the system as it is, imperfect as it is, people should know the rules of the game until a brand new system is in place and we have the gospel for this country's refugee policy. Instead we have one layer of bureaucracy on top of another, and the policy is being tinkered with every second or third day. In the end no one knows the direction the Government is taking, and certainly the refugees are getting conflicting signals.
By removing the B-l list, in theory at least we may be deporting people to countries which we, just 10 days ago, deemed dangerous because of real persecution. We are jeopardizing those people. We are driving people to protect themselves through hunger strikes. We are stranding people at airports.
Canada has had a tradition of helping refugees in their plight. We cannot take everyone. We cannot open our doors wide enough for all the world's refugees. No one is saying that. However, we have a role to play. Yet that role is becoming fuzzy simply because we are sending confusing signals, which in turn is because the system is not working well. We have the ability to eliminate the backlog and take care of those seeking refugee status and at the same time give Canadians confidence that the system has a degree of integrity and consistency and will protect their interests as well.
Adjournment Debate
What we in the Opposition are trying to say is, stop tinkering with the system. Stop sending up trial balloons and leave the system as it is until we can bring in a new and permanent system. I look forward to the Government agreeing with that principle and telling us when we can expect such a policy.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to respond to the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) concerning this very important issue. Last week, while the House was in recess, we had an opportunity to be in our ridings. It is not often that we get comments in our constituency offices about things which have been done well. However, the announcement made by the Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner) concerning changes in the refugee determination process was most positively received by the Canadian public.
I want to point out how welcome those changes were in my riding of Scarborough Centre. The changes were made to be fair to both the people coming into this country and those who live here now. Certainly we encourage refugees coming to Canada. The compassionate and humanitarian nature of both Canadians and this Government have never been questioned. The Nansen Medal which was awarded to the Canadian people is a great tribute to that compassion.
To specifically reply to the Hon. Member's comments, I wish to emphasize that the Government is satisfied that the current arrangement with the U.S. Government is providing the necessary protection against removal of a potential refugee claimant to a country where he or she alleges they will be at risk. The arrangement with the U.S. Government is that there will be a case-by-case review of each refugee claimant. Where there is no danger of immediate removal from the U.S., an immigration inquiry will be scheduled and the individual will remain in the U.S. until then. Where U.S. immigration indicates an individual is under deportation order and subject to immediate removal, the person will be allowed to enter Canada immediately to await the inquiry. Since those measures have been initiated there has been almost daily contact between the U.S. and Canadian officials at border crossings. There is evidence that American officials are cooperating to ensure that no potential refugee claimant will be removed from the U.S. prior to the date of the Canadian immigration inquiry.
I want to say to the Hon. Member that the administrative review was not an amnesty. Some 80 per cent of those reviewed have been allowed to stay in Canada. Some 20 per cent have not. That is not an amnesty. We are considering each case separately. We are not planning an amnesty as reported in The Globe and Mail. The Minister spoke very clearly about that in the House today. The fact is that we have not had an amnesty and are not planning one. Each case will be decided upon separately. I want to emphasize that Canada and the Government will treat each real, true refugee in a compassionate and humanitarian way, as is the Canadian way.

Let me reassure the Hon. Member that the concerns he expressed tonight about co-op housing and low rental housing in his riding are the same concerns expressed in the riding of LaSalle which I represent. We have the same problems that were caused by the former Liberal administration and we are trying to correct them.

Our Government's success in this field is a source of intense pride for us all and especially for the new Minister responsible for the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mclnnes). I welcome this
March 3, 1987

opportunity this evening to give some additional information on these programs.
In 1985, when government guidelines and housing programs were being reviewed, one of the guiding principles was to channel public funds to those who were most in need.
That is exactly what we have done. Now that a new set of programs, many administered jointly with the provinces, are being implemented, more truly needy Canadians are able to take advantage of Government assistance in obtaining affordable housing.

To help moderate income Canadians, those on the margin of ownership, a new co-operative housing program was developed to provide co-op members security of tenure through more effective use of public funds.

Furthermore, all housing co-ops must allocate a certain number of units for subsidized housing. Federal-provincial shared cost programs provide for rent geared to income in about 30 per cent of housing units for low-income Canadians.
Still on the subject of co-ops, if operating costs exceed market levels for rents, a subsidy is applied to make up the difference. Subsidies paid in subsequent years are normally indexed to the real rate of inflation. During the program review, the Co-operative Housing Foundation urged the Canadian Government to adopt an experimental mortgage instrument that had been used for some time, with considerable success, in Denmark. I am referring to an indexed
Adjournment Debate
mortgage loan, fully guaranteed by the mortgage loan insurance plan under the National Housing Act, which has been available for about six months.
The real interest rate hoped for by the Foundation did not materialize, unfortunately. Capital costs have soared, and last year's budget was not as flexible as the co-operative housing sector would have wished.
The Government of Canada continues to support the co-op form of tenure as an alternative for Canadians, and is watching with great concern the acceptance of this experimental mortgage instrument.

Our Government remains committed to channelling its limited resources to Canadians who are most in need.

That is to say our Canadian Government continues in its resolve to target its limited resources to helping those Canadians in greatest need in York East and in LaSalle.
